articles.content: In partnership with Michigan Public, The Moth Mainstage returns to the Wharton Center Friday evening, featuring a lineup of writers, performers and storytellers from Michigan and beyond. With the theme “Tightrope,” the show will focus on stories about what happens when the path forward is unclear. Maureen Abood. Courtesy East Lansing’s Maureen Abood is one of the evening’s storytellers. A Lebanese-American food writer, Abood’s interviews, stories and recipes have appeared in numerous outlets, including The New York Times, Food & Wine magazine and The Splendid Table. Lansing’s Andrea King Collier, an award-winning author, journalist and photographer whose work has been featured in The Oprah Magazine, Essence and Town & Country, will also perform. Tickets start at $40, with discounts for students, and are available online. The Moth Mainstage: Tightrope 7:30 p.m. Friday, Nov. 13 Wharton Center 750 E. Shaw Lane, East Lansing whartoncenter.com

articles.content: MSU Vinyl Nights, a student organization dedicated to building community through music and the preservation of physical media, is hosting a performance Friday evening by Lansing’s Anthony Jones-Player, also known simply as The Player. Attendees will have the chance to experience Jones-Player’s music in an intimate setting, similar to NPR’s Tiny Desk concerts. He will be backed by a band of student musicians, as well as background vocalists. A rapper, singer and songwriter, Jones-Player has been releasing music since 2018 but started writing when he was 8 years old. With over 120,000 streams across digital platforms, he has performed at venues like the Wharton Center and Grewal Hall and events like the annual Stoopfest. MSU Vinyl Nights 7 p.m. Friday, Nov. 13 Fourth floor, MSU Main Library 366 W. Circle Drive, East Lansing Free instagram.com/msuvinylnights

articles.title: ‘Eurydice’ flips a classic Greek myth on its head
articles.description: Lansing Community College’s production of “Eurydice,” by Sarah Ruhl, is a sumptuous reinterpretation of a classic Greek myth as a contemporary story of love, loss and sacrifice. The script is […]
articles.content: Lansing Community College’s production of “Eurydice,” by Sarah Ruhl, is a sumptuous reinterpretation of a classic Greek myth as a contemporary story of love, loss and sacrifice. The script is based loosely on the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice. In the Greek tale, Eurydice is bitten by a snake and dies soon after their wedding. A despondent Orpheus uses his preternatural musical talents to charm his way into the underworld to bring Eurydice back to the land of the living. Hades agrees to release her, with the caveat that Orpheus cannot look upon her until they have left the underworld. Unfortunately, Orpheus turns to look at her when he reaches the upper world, and because Eurydice has not yet crossed the threshold, she vanishes forever. A’Layah Houston as the titular character in LCC’s production of “Eurydice.” Photo by Cass Hopp Ruhl presents the narrative from Eurydice’s point of view and adds a new major character, shifting the focus of the story from Orpheus’ loss to an empowered Eurydice making choices that impact all around her. In Ruhl’s story, we meet Eurydice’s (A’Layah Houston) deceased Father (Mark Gmazel), who watches his daughter from the underworld. On her wedding day to Orpheus (Daedyn Lockhart), Father sends Eurydice a letter, which is intercepted by the Nasty Interesting Man (Will Jodloski). Nasty Interesting Man persuades Eurydice to come back to his penthouse apartment to retrieve the letter. When he tries to seduce her, she flees, trips on the stairs and falls to her death. In the underworld, dead people are dipped in the river Lethe, causing them to forget their lives and language. Father somehow avoided this fate, but Eurydice does not. A significant part of the play focuses on Father restoring Eurydice’s language and memories. The scenes between Houston and Gmazel are funny and touching, but be warned: This is a Greek tragedy. Ruhl brings the story to its inevitable conclusion, which is poignant and heartbreaking. “Eurydice” 7 p.m. Friday, Nov. 13-Saturday, Nov. 14 LCC Dart Auditorium 500 N. Capitol Ave., Lansing (517) 483-1122 lcc.edu/showinfo It’s almost a shame that LCC’s performances are free, because it becomes underwhelming to say that Jodloski’s and Gmazel’s performances alone are worth the price of admission. Gmazel’s Father is grounded, warm and comforting, while Lodloski’s Nasty Interesting Man and Lord of the Underworld — who are likely the same character — are cartoonishly yet very creepily menacing. While Gmazel is a seasoned actor who anchors the play with his naturalistic delivery and physicality, Jodloski is a first-year theater student who resists the adrenaline rush of being on stage and patiently holds his syllables a little longer than a human would be comfortable doing to portray his snaky, scary character. Ruhl’s Lord of the Underworld is childlike yet chilling, and in his last appearance as the “grown-up” version of the Lord, Jodloski is horror-film terrifying as he threatens to make Eurydice his bride. Dart Auditorium is a fine performance space with a generous stage and fantastic lighting equipment, allowing light designer Michael Beyer to create a rich landscape of blues and purples to fill in the otherwise spartan set. While the props are minimal, designer Anna Szabo adds a special Michigan touch by decorating Eurydice’s and her Father’s underworld accessories in a Petoskey stone pattern. Although the play starts out a bit slow, it becomes a very moving experience once Eurydice enters the underworld, highly recommended for daddies and daughters who are too old for those elementary school dances.

Riverwalk’s ‘Clybourne Park’ is no walk in the park
articles.description: Since the dawn of storytelling, conflict has been a necessary ingredient. Bruce Norris’ “Clybourne Park” is packed with conflict and tension from start to finish. Think of Riverwalk Theatre’s current […]
articles.content: Since the dawn of storytelling, conflict has been a necessary ingredient. Bruce Norris’ “Clybourne Park” is packed with conflict and tension from start to finish. Think of Riverwalk Theatre’s current black box show as an episode of “All in the Family,” but without the copious laughs. “Clybourne Park” opens in a mid-20th-century suburban Chicago home with a bickering couple, Bev and Russ, authentically performed by Joyce Kramer-Cox and Mike Stewart. It becomes obvious that a family tragedy has a lot to do with why they are so short tempered. And when Pastor Jim (played with the perfect amount of awkwardness by Ayden Soupal) visits their home to “help,” conversations become even more heated and profane. Joyce Kramer-Cox, Ayden Soupal, Paule Justin and Jordan Taylor in Riverwalk Theatre’s production of “Clybourne Park.” Photo by Ariniko Artistry Emotions rise to a peak when Karl (a distraught neighbor masterfully played by Joe Clark) rants and fumes about the sale of Bev and Russ’ house. It’s then confirmed that the central issue of the show is racism. Until then, Francine (Paule Justin), the Black maid, and her husband, Albert (Jordan Taylor), are mostly overly polite bystanders. When the couple convincingly begins to flinch at dialogue peppered with racist comments, the audience cringes along with them. Karl’s rudeness to his deaf and timid wife (persuasively portrayed by Sarah Lehman) is also difficult to witness. The increasing hostility between Francine and Albert on one side and Bev and Russ on the other amplifies the discomfort. “Clybourne Park” 7 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 12 8 p.m. Friday, Nov. 13-Saturday, Nov. 14 2 p.m. Sunday, Nov. 15 Riverwalk Theatre 228 Museum Drive, Lansing (517) 482-5700 riverwalktheatre.com After experiencing such an intense hour of conflict and odious remarks, the 20-minute intermission is a welcome respite. The second hour takes place in the remains of the house, 50 years later. The set is altered significantly, and the cast masterfully assumes very different roles. The friction between the couples and the underlying stench of racism still dominate their banter, but this time, a white couple is the target. If that isn’t enough to process, the show ends with a flashback to the family tragedy. As the son, Soupal manages to add sorrow to an already long list of uncomfortable emotions. But despite a heart-wrenching tragedy and sometimes cruel characters with repulsive prejudices, Riverwalk’s “Clybourne Park” is a must see. Sure, it can be incredibly hard to sit through, and its story can be bothersome — but that’s the point. The play is meant to disturb. It’s also meant to teach. And with genius dialogue that often wanders in cleverly annoying directions and superb actors who expertly embody their characters (including just-right facial expressions), the production is award worthy. “Clybourne Park” may not be a sitcom with lots of lighthearted moments that suit canned laughter. But it has all the makings of good theater: powerful acting, direction, script and set. And, of course, conflict.

articles.title: Peppermint Creek’s ‘Witch’ hits home at the right time
articles.description: Peppermint Creek Theatre Co. has the supernatural power of programming its plays to hit when current events match the themes of the work. It’s downright spooky how relevant its shows […]
articles.content: Peppermint Creek Theatre Co. has the supernatural power of programming its plays to hit when current events match the themes of the work. It’s downright spooky how relevant its shows are, and its production of “Witch” is no exception. The play opens in a tavern in Edmonton, a remote, semi-rural medieval village where the charismatic Scratch (Lewis C. Elson) is buying souls. His first client is Cuddy (Hannah Zwolensky), the only son of the town’s lord, who is more interested in folk dancing than following in his father’s footsteps. Sir Arthur (Jeff Magnuson) has taken in Frank (Ndegwa McCloud), a robust young man whom he admires more than his son. Ndegwa McCloud (left) and Jeff Magnuson in Peppermint Creek Theatre Co.’s production of “Witch.” Photo by Trumpie Photography Cuddy is threatened by Frank’s ambition and sells his soul to have Frank killed. Scratch then makes a deal with Frank, who wants to be named Sir Arthur’s heir. The conflicting deals create great tension throughout the play. Meanwhile, we learn that Sir Arthur’s servant girl Winnifred (Storm Hawthorn) is secretly married to Frank, which puts his ambitions at risk. Scratch hears about a town witch and seeks her out to forge another deal. Elizabeth (Abby Perry) is not a witch, but she is a single, independent woman and is therefore suspect for anything that goes wrong with farm animals, crops and people. Scratch meets his match in this strong-willed woman, and they soon become unlikely friends. Back at the manor, tensions rise between Cuddy and Frank, revealing the true love-hate nature of their relationship. A major theme about toxic masculinity emerges, and the rivalry reaches a shocking climax. Sir Arthur is also a victim of toxic masculinity. Magnuson nails the role of the shallow ruler, a clueless man who can’t imagine dismantling the social structure that he himself inherited, even to save his relationship with Cuddy. When left alone to converse with his dead wife, he becomes a lost manchild whose strength came from her. Scratch delivers a powerful speech about gender inequality, and his acknowledgement that there is inherent value in being male further reinforces the theme. As Scratch grows closer to Elizabeth, he becomes emotionally invested in her fate, and his final soliloquy moves us to have sympathy for this devil. “Witch” 7 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 12-Saturday, Nov. 14 3 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 14-Sunday, Nov. 15 Stage One 2200 Lake Lansing Road, Lansing (517) 927-3016 peppermintcreek.org Playwright Jen Silverman structured the script in an interesting way. The scenes primarily flip back and forth from Sir Arthur’s bustling manor to Elizabeth’s isolated cottage. Elizabeth remains isolated from the other characters until Winnifred seeks out Scratch at her cottage. It is this vital, heart-wrenching, woman-to-woman conversation that gives Elizabeth clarity on the one thing she is willing to sell her soul for. Peppermint Creek’s theme for this season is “what we want/what it costs,” and “Witch” fits that theme well. Every character wants something: Sir Arthur wants an heir, Frank wants material success, Cuddy wants his father’s love, Winnifred wants Frank’s love, and Scratch wants their souls. As for Elizabeth? It’s her journey toward realizing what she wants, what she is willing to sell her soul for, that’s at the heart of the play. Another timely theme is that greed destroys. As Scratch says, “Once you have everything, you just want more,” something we see playing out in the real world among the billionaire oligarch class and our federal administration. In the microcosm of “Witch,” Elizabeth alone recognizes that the cycles of greed and toxic masculinity have broken their world, and she alone can change the world, perhaps suggesting an additional theme about the responsibility of the individual in making their world a better place for all. Director Sally Hecksel selected an entertaining and important play that hits home at the right time. As the nation faces the opportunity to build a better world, “Witch” reminds us that change comes at a cost, which may include personal sacrifice.

articles.title: ‘You’ve Got Mail’ Reboot in the Works at Warner Bros.
articles.description: The film from director Jason Orley will be a new take on the original 1998 rom-com starring Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan.
articles.content: The film from director Jason Orley will be a new take on the original 1998 rom-com starring Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan. A new take on the beloved rom-com You’ve Got Mail is in the works at Warner Bros., The Hollywood Reporter has learned. Rather than a remake of the original 1998 film starring Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan, the new film will follow a new story, though plot details are being kept under wraps. Jason Orley (Close Personal Friends, Bupkis and I Want You Back) has been tapped to direct the project. He’s also writing the current draft based on a screenplay by Deborah Kaplan and Harry Elfont. Neal Moritz and Tania Landau from the original movie are also returning to produce. Related Stories Business Pam Abdy Laments Exits of Top Female Executives in Hollywood: "It Is Upsetting to See" Movies DC Studios' James Gunn and Peter Safran Recall Detailing Long-Term Plans to New Boss David Ellison The 1998 pic, based on Miklós László’s 1937 Hungarian play Parfumerie, follows book superstore magnate Joe Fox (Hanks) and independent book shop owner Kathleen Kelly (Ryan) as they fall in love in the anonymity of the Internet. However, they’re both blissfully unaware that he’s trying to put her out of business. Greg Kinnear, Parker Posey, Jean Stapleton, Steve Zahn, Heather Burns and Dave Chappelle also starred in the film helmed by Nora Ephron. Upon its release, You’ve Got Mail grossed more than $250 million at the global box office, not adjusted for inflation. It became Ephron’s highest-grossing film to date, behind Sleepless in Seattle (1993). Ryan also earned a Golden Globe nomination the following year for best actress in a motion picture — comedy or musical for her performance as Kathleen. Orley is repped by UTA, Rise Management and Hansen, Jacobson, Teller, Hoberman, Newman, Warren, Richman, Rush, Kaller, & Gellman L.L.P. How to make a beat: When schools were losing arts programming, Ozay Moore put his life in hip-hop to work for Lansing’s next generation
articles.description: Step 1: Dig in the crates Every good beat begins with listening. In 2008, my crates were YouTube videos: West Coast underground hip-hop, freestyle sessions, cyphers. One discovery led to […]
articles.content: Step 1: Dig in the crates Every good beat begins with listening. In 2008, my crates were YouTube videos: West Coast underground hip-hop, freestyle sessions, cyphers. One discovery led to another. The Procussions. Then Lightheaded, whose sample-heavy boom bap paired classic hip-hop rhythms with positive lyrics. Within that sound, I found an emcee named Othello. His second album, “Live at the Assembly Line,” led me to his MySpace page, where he’d announced he was moving to Lansing. Of all places. Years later, I would understand what a lifetime in hip-hop could offer a city whose young people were losing opportunities to create. Ozay Moore Moore with his wife, Rebekah Pumphrey. Courtesy Step 2: Find your sample Before he was Ozay Moore, founder of All of the Above Hip Hop Academy, he was Othello, a rapper who was signed to a record label at 18 and toured internationally, including on the Warped Tour, while raising a newborn with his wife. Touring meant booking shows, building relationships and surviving between gigs. When Moore and his wife moved to Lansing to be closer to family, he brought those experience with him. Moore had moved to Michigan to work, but budget cuts were drying up that work. The same cuts threatening his livelihood were also taking teachers and arts programming out of schools. All of the Above Hip Hop Academy emerged from that shared uncertainty. He remembers thinking, “Use what I know for something. They’re pulling P.E. teachers out of the schools; the arts are suffering. Man, what if we stepped in with hip-hop-based programming?” A cut to an arts program means fewer chances to pick up an instrument, write something or find an adult who takes your creativity seriously. The need for those experiences doesn’t disappear with the funding. Step 3: Find the break On Michigan State University’s campus, Moore found Code of the Cutz, a hip-hop shop owned by Jaime Wilkins (DJ AddVerse). It sold records, graffiti paint and supplies. Freestyle cyphers brought people together there. So did conversations about Darfur. Through his work with Ingham Academy and Detroit Public Schools, Moore had been gaining experience in teaching and developing programs. At Code of the Cutz, he saw another kind of learning happen around records, paint and cyphers. When the shop closed around 2007, Greater Lansing lost another gathering place. Executive director Ozay Moore (center right, in khaki) at the 2024 grand opening of All of the Above Hip Hop Academy in downtown Lansing. Courtesy Step 4: Flip the sample Moore took the energy of Code of the Cutz and mixed it with his years of touring, booking and teaching. The result was All of the Above Hip Hop Academy. An afterschool program, The Cook Up, pairs students with local teaching artists in beat making, rhyme writing, graffiti, breaking and DJing. They get lessons on all that, but the biggest lesson is learning how to use the pool of resources and skills to make school and life better. Moore had to take several odd jobs to survive between shows and tours. Working artists have knowledge to share, but they also have bills to pay. All of the Above helps create paid opportunities for local artists to mentor students while continuing their own careers and fostering the next generation. After all, what’s more hip-hop than taking the best of the scraps you have and creating something big and dope for the community? All of the Above executive director Ozay Moore emcees a past Cap City Jam. Courtesy Step 5: Leave room for another verse Moore still raps, but these days, being an executive director, husband and father takes priority. He smiles when he talks about The Player, an artist from The Cook Up: his consistency, his desire to get better, his willingness to put himself out there. The Player has released projects consistently since 2020 and rocked shows at The Robin Theatre and the Wharton Center. Look around town and you’ll probably find a flyer for an event he’s hosting. I’ve been on the receiving end of that mentorship, too. As I built The Poetry Room, Moore became someone I could ask about grants, boards and programming. He helped me land my first paid gig. The artist I’d discovered online had become someone helping me make room for other artists. We talk about running organizations. Sometimes we just talk about obscure hip-hop history that only a couple of heads would remember. Ozay Moore poses with spray paint can in hand in front of one of his pieces. – Courtesy Step 6: Let the beat build Eighteen years ago, Moore had no idea that anyone in Lansing was listening, or that we’d become peers in building spaces for the next generation. Back then, I wondered why someone like Othello would move to Lansing. Now I wonder who’s been listening to us, watching our moves. And what they’ll create next.

Local watercolor artist illustrates best-selling book about cats
articles.description: Artist Michelle Detering has illustrated book covers before, but never an entire book from start to finish — until the recently released “I’m Still Here: A Cat’s Purpose Forever” (Andrews McMeel […]
articles.content: Artist Michelle Detering has illustrated book covers before, but never an entire book from start to finish — until the recently released “I’m Still Here: A Cat’s Purpose Forever” (Andrews McMeel Publishing, $19.99), written by Cathryn Michon. “There were close to 80 illustrations that needed to be completed in a relatively short period of time. That meant that every day for months, I spent long hours in the studio painting. It was intense,” Detering said. Michelle Detering The book is told from the point of view of a cat. It gently reminds grieving owners that the unique bond shared with a cat never fades, blending free-verse poetry with subtle humor regarding a cat’s “superior” view of the universe. “Cathryn contacted me after seeing my Instagram account and the cat portraits I’ve done in the past,” Detering said. “She reached out to me and asked if I would be interested in illustrating her sequel to ‘I’m Still Here: A Dog’s Purpose Forever.’ We had a Zoom call to discuss the details, and then another with the publisher, and I was hired!” She really enjoyed the experience and learned a lot about illustration work. “You have to be able to paint what the author’s vision is. This can be a challenge sometimes because what you think might be great for a particular page may not be what the author or editor thinks works. So, sometimes I would have to go back and do another version of an illustration, one that was closer to what Cathryn was thinking,” Detering explained. “Cathryn is a movie director as well, so she was very helpful with describing through storyboards what she wanted each page to look like. Basically, I would read the text and look at her storyboards and paint how I thought the illustration should look. Sometimes there would be changes or redos that needed to be done, and sometimes they were perfect on the first pass.” For six months, Detering and Michon communicated on a daily basis via phone calls, texts, emails and Zoom meetings. “Cathryn and I had a lot of interaction — I think more than many illustrators do with the author. She lives in Los Angeles, so I’ve never actually met her in person. We still continue to communicate on a semi-regular basis to this day,” Detering said. “I enjoy challenges, and each day presented itself with a new painting to work on, which brought with it the fun of painting something new and the challenge of trying to fit it in with the text and vision.” The artist gave her perspective on what makes “I’m Still Here” stand out from other books about pets. “I think what’s different about it is that it’s an inclusive book for all ages, using poetic storytelling and rich illustrations to celebrate the connection we have with our cats, even after they’re gone,” she said. “This book is really beautifully made. It’s a book that you can pick up anytime to make you smile or shed a tear remembering the good times and love you shared with your cat. These things, I think, are what landed the book on the Los Angeles Times’ best-sellers list.” Born in Lansing, Detering is the youngest of two. She lives in Holt with her husband of 23 years, Jeff Janowick, who’s a history professor at Lansing Community College. After graduating from high school in the Lansing area, she earned both a bachelor’s degree in dietetics and a master’s degree in education from Michigan State University. She also completed coursework in art and design at LCC. “I’ve loved art and design since I was little. My mom was an artist and always encouraged me to be creative. I love expressing something in a pleasing and visual way — a language without words,” she said. “I did photography in high school and really enjoyed it. I love to travel and to be in nature. Photography allows me to capture those memories of a moment in time. Photography is capturing a moment, and painting is like reinterpreting that moment to say even more.” Her love of watercolor began with a course she took at LCC. “I love the fluidity and transparency of watercolor,” she said. “It’s soft and ethereal, which I think helps capture a more otherworldly effect. I also like the challenge of not being able to correct mistakes in the same way you can with oil or acrylic because of its transparency. It requires a combination of creative thinking, skill from practice and a bit of magic.” One highlight of Detering’s career is having her artwork appear in an issue of British Vogue with singer Taylor Swift gracing the cover. “The Vogue magazine appearance was the first time I had seen my work in print in a worldwide publication. It was kind of mind blowing to go to the bookstore and open a magazine to see my painting in there,” she said. Detering has been a full-time artist for 11 years. Previously, she was an academic advisor at LCC, although she created art on the side. “About 12 years ago, I received a billboard with my artwork through the Greater Lansing Arts Council. That sort of catapulted my career. People started to want to buy my work, and I was getting busier and busier with that. I thought to myself, ‘I could do this for a full-time job!’ she recalled. “I started an Etsy shop and began participating in summer art fairs. I realized that I could really do this, so I decided to leave my full-time job at LCC to try to make a living at it. I’ve loved every minute of it since.” Visit michelledeteringart.com and instagram.com/michelle_detering_art.

articles.title: More than a dozen key races remain too early to call one week after Election Day
articles.description: More than a dozen key races remain too early to call one week after Election Day AP News Hello, More Democratic Senators. Bye-Bye, Lauren Boebert? Slate Magazine Some House and Senate races remain uncalled. What we know NPR Lots of 2026 midterm races haven’t been called yet. Here’s where things stand right now. Yahoo Where all 16 unprojected House races stand The Hill
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — The size of Democrats’ majorities in the House and Senate remained undetermined one week after Election Day as more than a dozen races were still too early to call Tuesday. Democrats are on track to hold 54 Senate seats in January, but could pick up one or two more from Republicans as votes are counted in Alaska and Mississippi. With 255 seats in the House, Democrats will have their largest majority elected to the chamber since 2008, with the potential to pick up several more seats as the remaining races are called. Here’s a look at where things stand in some of the uncalled races: Late in the afternoon Tuesday, Democrat Scott Colom was about 2,600 votes ahead of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the race for Senate in Mississippi. There are two key deadlines in the vote-counting process in Mississippi this week: Mail-in absentee ballots must be received by Tuesday, and counties are required to submit their certified election results — including tallies of provisional ballots — to the state by Friday. It is unclear exactly how many ballots are left to count. Unlike in some other states, there is no central vote reporting system for Mississippi, and few counties release election results online. Instead, Associated Press journalists and analysts communicate with each of the state’s 82 counties directly for the latest available information on vote counts. The state will certify its results on Dec. 3. On Monday, Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said about 14,200 provisional ballots had been processed, of which about 80% were accepted, and about 2,700 mail-in absentee ballots had not yet been returned. Mississippi does not have automatic recounts or permit candidates to request a recount. Recounts in the state are held only in the event of a court order. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is eligible for a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome. Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by about 2,500 votes in Alaska’s Senate race on Tuesday afternoon, with an estimated 76% of the vote counted. The results of some absentee ballots are expected to be released late Tuesday, though the final absentee ballots mailed back from outside the U.S. are accepted as late as Nov. 18, 15 days after Election Day. Ranked choice voting could also affect the timeline. Peltola is just over 1 percentage point short of the majority needed to win outright. If neither candidate wins a majority, the race will proceed to ranked choice tabulation on Nov. 18. The state’s “target date” for certifying the election results is Nov. 25. Recounts in Alaska are automatic only in the event of a tie vote. Candidates may also request a recount within five days of the state’s certification. In most of the House races that have not been called, the margin between the leading candidates was less than 1 percentage point among votes counted as of late Tuesday afternoon. In North Carolina, four races remain undecided, the most of any state, and Republican incumbents were being challenged in all. There are no automatic recounts in North Carolina, but candidates may request a recount if the margin between candidates is 1% or less of the total votes. The state must receive the recount request by noon Eastern time Nov. 17, two business days after the county canvass in the state. The state is scheduled to certify its results Nov. 24. In California, only one of the remaining House races, in the 23rd District, will affect the chamber’s balance of power. The other uncalled race is between two Democrats. Mail ballots must be received by Tuesday and counties must certify their results Dec. 3. The state will certify its results Dec. 11. In South Carolina’s 2nd District, a recount is ongoing in the race between Republican incumbent Joe Wilson and Democrat Zyon Khalia. Wilson led Khalia by only about 3,000 votes in the original tally by late Tuesday afternoon, when 99% of the votes had been counted. In Minnesota’s 1st District, the race was still undecided late in the afternoon Tuesday, with about 300 votes separating the top two candidates and an estimated 99% of votes counted. Recounts are not automatic in Minnesota, but a candidate can request a publicly-funded recount if the margin between the winning and losing candidates is less than 0.25% of the vote. In Tennessee’s 4th District, about 300 votes lay between Democrat Victoria Broderick and Republican incumbent Scott DesJarlais as of late afternoon Tuesday. In that state, recounts are held only as part of a legal challenge in the courts. There are no automatic recounts, and losing candidates may not request recounts. Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher led state Republican Senate President Ty Masterson in the race for governor of Kansas by less than 1 percentage point late Tuesday afternoon. On Nov. 4, the state announced that a close-race audit of election results requiring a hand count of selected ballots had been triggered in six close Kansas races, including the gubernatorial race. The audit must be completed before Nov. 16, the day by which counties must certify their results. In the race for governor of Alaska, only about 76% of votes were estimated to had been counted late Tuesday afternoon, and the Democratic candidate, Jonathan S. Kreiss‑Tomkins, was leading Bernadette M. Wilson by about 45,000 votes, 49.6% to 28.9%. The race will advance to ranked choice tabulation if no candidate receives more than 50% of votes.

articles.title: Money out of Politics campaign wants in on lawsuit defense
articles.description: Utility companies and the Mackinac Center for Public Policy are both suing in federal court to stop a voter-approved ballot measure from curbing political giving by big state contractors.
articles.content:
A person sits in attendance at a Michigan Board of State Canvassers meeting on August 17, 2026.

(Colin Jackson / Michigan Public Radio Network)The campaign behind a successful Michigan ballot measure wants to defend its work in court.If it stands after election results become final and legal challenges run their course, the policy will limit campaign donations from regulated utilities and large state government contractors. It will also set new transparency rules for political messaging.Public utilities and the Mackinac Center for Public Policy are both suing in federal court to stop it from taking effect. They’re citing First Amendment free-speech concerns.The lawsuits name Michigan government officials as the defendants. But the Michiganders for Money out of Politics campaign argues it should have a say in defending its work — a process called “intervening.”“The proposed intervenors have very distinct interests that are not the same as the state because they are regulated by Proposal 2, and they participate in the political process that’s going to be governed by Proposal 2,” the group’s lawyer, Sam Bagenstos, said Tuesday.Money out of Politics, sometimes referred to as Mop Up Michigan, filed a motion to intervene as a defendant in both cases this week. The group is including Democratic state Rep.-elect Joanna Whaley as part of its filing.Bagenstos said that because the incoming lawmaker and the members of the coalition groups personally deal with the political system, they’ll bring a perspective the state can’t offer.“They want to have access to the disclosures of independent expenditures that will be required by Proposal 2. They want to participate in the political process where regulated utilities can’t skew that process,” Bagenstos said.While Bagnestos is arguing for intervention, attorneys for the Mackinac Center for Public Policy don’t see a need.Patrick Wright is the center’s vice president for legal affairs.“Once the law becomes the law, it’s the state of Michigan’s law. It’s no longer Mop Up Michigan’s law, or it doesn’t have really any ownership stake in it anymore,” Wright said.He argued it shouldn’t matter that Michiganders for Money Out of Politics sponsored the law change.“There is really nothing unique that any of these groups that are attempting to get in offer that the attorney general’s not going to argue in defense of this law,” Wright said.The judge in the Mackinac Center lawsuit is asking for a reply by November 20.A state elections board is scheduled to meet on November 23 to finalize the results of the election.The measure is written to become law 10 days after its win at the ballot box is certified. That means, without a court delay, it could begin taking effect as soon as early December.The utility-led lawsuit has already asked the courts to temporarily block the proposal from being enforced. Wright said the Mackinac Center plans to do the same.

Senate Republicans vote to keep John Thune as leader after steep election losses
articles.description: Senate Republicans vote to keep John Thune as leader after steep election losses AP News Thune elected Senate GOP leader after bruising showdown with critics The Hill Pressure builds on Thune ahead of GOP leadership elections Axios RNC members call for delay in congressional leadership elections after midterm losses Politico Thune and Schumer face questions about Senate leadership in aftermath of elections AP News
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Republicans reelected South Dakota Sen. John Thune as their leader Tuesday after a tense day of private discussions about steep losses in the midterm elections that cost them their majority. Thune was always expected to prevail, as he is popular with his GOP colleagues and was running unopposed in the secret-ballot election. But Senate Republicans vented their frustrations in three separate meetings Tuesday after an election wipeout that cost them at least seven Senate seats. Some Republicans had tried to delay the leadership decision, but the conference voted 31-15 to proceed with a vote after Thune made his case to his colleagues, laying out his vision for the minority and also promising that they will try and do as much as they can in their final two months in the majority. “We’re going to make the most of the time we’ve got,” Thune said after he was elected by acclamation, without a roll call vote. As for next year, Thune said that told his colleagues that they will “come out swinging, and realize we’ve got a lot of work to be done to get back in the majority.” The day’s meetings were a combination of venting and thoughtful conversation, with some senators who won and lost elections this year sharing their thoughts and others questioning if they should be quickly endorsing their leadership slate after a significant defeat. West Virginia Sen. Jim Justice said that there was a “legitimate argument that, good gracious, if we lost as badly as we lost, why would we continue on with the same leadership?” At the same time, the current GOP leadership “didn’t cause this problem to happen,” Justice said. “They do a good job.” Republicans’ angst and indecision come as frustrated Republicans are just beginning to reckon with what the election results mean for their future — and for their relationship with President Donald Trump, as voters resoundingly rejected their two years of single-party rule in Congress and the White House. Two additional Senate races remain uncalled in Alaska and Mississippi that could further deplete their numbers. “If you don’t think after losing seven Senate seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” said Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley, who voted to delay the elections. He said he wasn’t aware of anyone else running for leader, but “maybe there would be” if they waited. Thune, who replaced Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky as leader in early 2025, pushed back on the idea of a delay, questioning what it would achieve. Several senators backed him up, including his South Dakota colleague Mike Rounds, who countered the calls for postponement with the successful motion to vote immediately. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, who was reelected to her leadership position as GOP policy chair, said that Thune wasn’t the reason they suffered losses. “I don’t think it was the fault of our leadership, quite frankly,” she said. Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., said he had confidence in the newly re-elected slate. The discussion was mainly “about policy,” he said. Republicans in the meeting were also pushing Thune to stay in session around the clock in the coming weeks to push through war spending and other party priorities before they lose power in January. Republicans are trying to wrap up the year’s work — funding the government, confirming Trump’s nominees and seeing if there are some issues where they can work with Democrats, including an energy permitting bill that moved forward on a bipartisan vote Monday evening. Before the vote on Thune, the conference adopted a resolution to maximize the time they have left and to “confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of.” “We need a plan to get the Republican agenda done,” said Florida Sen. Rick Scott. Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson circulated a letter before the meeting asking for the delay. He said the conference needs to do some “real soul-searching” but also conceded that there was no one else on the ballot. “That’s part of our problem, who would want the job?” he said on Monday, turning to a reporter and joking, “Do you want it?” Oklahoma Sen. Jim Lankford said that there was “widespread support” among Republican senators for Thune, who has made it a point to hear out different viewpoints before he makes major decisions and has maintained close relationships with the rank and file — a different approach from his predecessor, McConnell. Lankford said he supported having the elections on Tuesday because many of the new GOP senators were already in town for freshman orientation. “It’s a pretty complicated role to be able to manage,” Lankford said of Thune’s leadership post. “No one wants that job.” Thune has spent much of the last two years navigating Trump, who has often been at odds with the Senate. While backing Trump on most policies, Thune has refused to change Senate rules and scrap the filibuster to pass voting legislation that would require proof of citizenship for all voters — a position that frustrated Trump and enraged some in the president’s political base. Still, Trump hosted Thune and his family at the White House in October. He said Monday that the GOP leader is “a very fine man.” The election is “up to the Senate,” Trump said. Thune has emphasized his collaborative approach to his colleagues and pointed out what they did get done in the last two years — including Trump’s sweeping tax and spending cuts legislation and an attempt at reining in the chaotic annual spending process. “We’re not going to be running this place next year, the Democrats are,” Thune said afterward. “But you can be assured that we will be very, very active in asserting conservative priorities.”

articles.title: US House GOP blocks effort to impeach Hegseth
articles.description: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has survived an impeachment effort, at least for now, after the U.S. House on Tuesday blocked a vote over charges that the Cabinet official oversaw extrajudicial killings and an illegal war against Iran. The House voted 211-204, largely along party lines, to refer articles of impeachment against Hegseth to a committee […]
articles.content: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth testifies during a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on Capitol Hill on July 21, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Finn Gomez/Getty Images)Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has survived an impeachment effort, at least for now, after the U.S. House on Tuesday blocked a vote over charges that the Cabinet official oversaw extrajudicial killings and an illegal war against Iran. The House voted 211-204, largely along party lines, to refer articles of impeachment against Hegseth to a committee — effectively killing the impeachment effort until the end of the current Congress in January. Eleven Democrats and seven Republicans missed the vote. The vote came hours after Hegseth defended himself in a fiery news conference at the Pentagon, where he denounced the impeachment effort as an attack on American service members. He called the bid to remove him a “farce” and flatly rejected the notion that he had committed impeachable offenses as the top civilian leader of the military. He likened himself to President Donald Trump, who was twice impeached during his first term. “Let’s be clear about what this resolution actually does. It tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations,” Hegseth said. Rep. Thomas Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, introduced articles of impeachment Monday alleging the Defense secretary waged unlawful war against Iran, ordered extrajudicial killings and ignored laws intended to minimize civilian casualties, among other charges. Impeachment would have represented an extraordinary rebuke of one of the most divisive members of Trump’s Cabinet. Hegseth, a 46-year-old former Fox News personality who narrowly won Senate confirmation last year, has sought to project a swashbuckling, masculine image as the military’s top civilian leader. He has rebranded the Department of Defense as the “Department of War,” purged numerous high-ranking officers and tried to kick critical media outlets out of the Pentagon. On Tuesday, Hegseth called Massie a “disgruntled and defeated congressman” who is attempting a “political spectacle” driven by ego and resentment. Massie, who has often clashed with Trump, lost his primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger. “It’s a farce and it’s a stunt and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said. Hegseth’s opponents could try again to impeach him during the new Congress, which begins in January. Democrats will hold a large majority in the House at that time. Earlier in the day, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who will likely become majority leader when his party takes over the chamber, said Hegseth should stand trial in the Senate if impeached. “Hegseth is already trying to hide behind our troops, falsely claiming that Congress disapproves of our courageous servicemembers even though we have fought to bring them home for months,” Schumer said. President Donald Trump has so far stood by Hegseth. He praised the Defense secretary in multiple public remarks over the past two weeks, saying he’s “done a fantastic job” in reducing the number of “woke” four-star generals, and for conducting the “war with Venezuela,” which he said “was over in 48 minutes.” “Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached. Congress, stand up for Pete!!!” Trump wrote in a social media post on Monday.

articles.content: Seagate doesn't think hybrid drives are done just yet. On Tuesday, the company announced the launch of the new FireCuda Forge line of storage drives. The FireCuda Forge is available right now through Seagate's web store, and comes in 8TB ($699) or 20TB ($899) HDD configurations—neither of which includes the required SSD. Users will have to bring their own SSD, with some specific restrictions. The FireCuda Forge is compatible with M.2 2280 NVMe drives that are PCIe Gen3 or higher. The maximum supported NVMe capacity is 1TB, which means that's as much data as you'll be able to dedicate to storage on the "fast side" of the hybrid setup. The NVMe will require minimum speeds of 2,400MB/s read and 2,000MB/s write, and a unit with DRAM cache is recommended. articles.title: Schumer ‘confident’ he’ll lead US Senate Dems despite criticism
articles.description: WASHINGTON — U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer said Tuesday he’s “confident” he will be reelected as Democratic leader for the next Congress, despite opposition from prominent members who argue he isn’t up to the task. While no one has publicly announced they will challenge Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, Maryland Sen. Chris Van […]
articles.content: U.S. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer speaks with reporters in the Capitol on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer said Tuesday he’s “confident” he will be reelected as Democratic leader for the next Congress, despite opposition from prominent members who argue he isn’t up to the task. While no one has publicly announced they will challenge Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen hasn’t ruled out the possibility. “What I’ve said is that we should not have a coronation,” Van Hollen said. “We should not support anybody for leader without a very clear plan. And as you know, there are many people who think a change is required.” Van Hollen said he was “actively listening” to other Democrats, but said he wasn’t inclined to make any announcements at this time. U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., in February 2025. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters) Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin and Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders, who caucuses with Democrats, said at a press conference they don’t support Schumer as leader. “I think whoever wants to run this caucus should come forward with a plan on how they’re going to govern differently, what they’re going to do in the first 100 days to put money in people’s pockets and then in particular how they’re going to communicate differently,” Slotkin said, adding she did not intend to challenge Schumer. She said leadership must “govern for the entirety of the caucus — for folks from blue states, purple states and red states.” Sanders said he was firmly opposed to Schumer. Slotkin said she is a no vote until she sees “a concrete plan that is definitely different.” Senate Democrats will have at least 54 seats next year after winning seats in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas, all of which are now held by a Republican. Democratic candidates also appear on track to win election in Alaska and Mississippi, though that could change as final votes are counted in the days ahead. Schumer declined to directly answer a question about whether he has spoken to Van Hollen since he began mulling a challenge. “Chris Van Hollen and I are friends,” he said. “We talk frequently and we’re united, united in lowering costs, united in ending this damn war” in Iran. But Schumer said he was “confident” he would be reelected when Senate Democrats gather behind closed doors this year to choose their leadership.

articles.title: US Senate GOP leader Thune reelected for next 2 years even after election losses
articles.description: WASHINGTON — South Dakota Sen. John Thune will remain Republican leader next Congress despite the GOP’s loss of the chamber’s majority in this year’s midterm elections. GOP senators voted behind closed doors Tuesday to keep Thune at the helm and reelected Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso as their whip. Neither was challenged. The other members of […]
articles.content: U.S. Senate Republican Leader John Thune, of South Dakota, speaks to reporters during a press conference in the Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — South Dakota Sen. John Thune will remain Republican leader next Congress despite the GOP’s loss of the chamber’s majority in this year’s midterm elections. GOP senators voted behind closed doors Tuesday to keep Thune at the helm and reelected Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso as their whip. Neither was challenged. The other members of Senate Republican leadership will include Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton of Arkansas, Republican Policy Committee Chair Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, Vice Chair of the Republican Conference James Lankford of Oklahoma and National Republican Senatorial Committee Chair Bernie Moreno of Ohio. ‘Listening intently’ Thune said after the meeting that he and other Republicans were not happy with the results of the midterm elections but will focus more on voters’ concerns in the years ahead. “As we move forward, we are going to be listening intently to what the American people are saying,” he said. “And I think right now the issue that matters the most to them, like I said, is the cost of living.” Thune pledged to extend the lame duck session that spans November and December to give Republicans more time to confirm nominees and approve legislation before handing over power to Democrats in early January. Republicans now hold 53 seats and The Associated Press projects they will have 44 next year, with results in Alaska and Mississippi still not called. “Our conference is committed to being here to do whatever it takes to get as much done as we can,” he said. “That means extending the calendar here, the number of days we’re here, the number of hours we’re here, the number of votes we may end up taking. But we are going to finish this legislative session strong.” Push for nominations There was an attempt by several Republican senators to delay decisions about leadership for at least a week, but they were ultimately unsuccessful. Missouri Sen. Eric Schmitt said after the meeting that Republican leaders had committed to clear as many nominees through the chamber as possible. Democrats are unlikely to approve President Donald Trump’s picks for the federal bench or administration roles after January. “We’re definitely going to maximize the next 54 days for sure,” he said. Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley said ahead of the vote that he wanted to delay until later this year to give Republicans an opportunity to “change course” following the election results. “It’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here,” he said, questioning why Republican leaders didn’t put bills on the floor to lower the cost of gasoline and healthcare. “If you don’t put people first, sooner or later people turn on you,” Hawley said. “And I think that this party thought we can just do whatever we want. People voted for us in ’24, we’ll do whatever we want. No you can’t. You’ve got to do stuff that actually helps people.” ‘Never disappoint voters again’ Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson said following a morning conference meeting that Republicans were “voicing opinions on all sides of the issues.” “It’s one of those times in the Republican Conference, you kind of go, ‘We got … some smart people, and we’re having a very good respectful conversation,’” Johnson said. Ohio Republican U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno speaks with reporters at the Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom) Ohio’s Moreno said later in the day that Republicans are committed to “never disappoint voters again.” “We’re firmly aware of the consequences now, and that’s the strategy we’re going to employ in 2028,” he said. 60 votes needed Thune will still have considerable power as minority leader as long as Democrats keep a rule that requires 60 senators vote to advance legislation. The hurdle forces bipartisanship on major proposals. But even if Democrats were to remove it next Congress, bills would still need Trump’s support to become law, unless there are supermajorities in each chamber to override a veto.

articles.description: Police investigate whether burned Ohio State University students were victims of hazing AP News 'Poor boy who is screaming': More details emerge in OSU fraternity fire incident WSYX Hazing investigation underway over Ohio State video, police records reveal The Columbus Dispatch Update: SAE investigated for hazing, victims from weekend incident suffer second- and third-degree burns The Lantern Ohio State Suspends Frat
articles.content: COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — Police are investigating whether two Ohio State University students who were treated for deep burns after being engulfed in flames at an outdoor fraternity party were victims of hazing. The university placed the Sigma Alpha Epsilon fraternity on interim suspension after a video circulated on social media showing a large group surrounding two young men on fire Saturday. A student who watched the video called police the next day to report a possible hazing incident, according to an audio recording of the call. “They stood around watching while this kid just burned,” said the student, who was sent the video in a group chat with her sorority members. The video shows a ring of people standing outside, many wearing the school’s red and white colors, laughing and shouting at two men on the ground with their pants on fire. One lunges at the other, and they both roll on the ground. The shouting takes on a more panicked tone as they struggle to remove their clothing. One onlooker holds a small fire extinguisher but doesn’t successfully deploy it. According to the Columbus Police report, the victims were both students who were treated for “moderate” second- and third-degree burns. The university has not said how the fraternity is linked to the event, but the report lists the president of the fraternity as part of the investigation. The report also lists hazing as the charge being investigated and notes that university authorities also are looking into whether hazing occurred. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine signed “Collin’s Law” in 2021 toughening penalties for hazing in the wake of a student’s death at a fraternity house at Ohio University. The law’s definition of hazing includes participating in or coercing anyone into behavior that creates a substantial risk of mental or physical harm and is tied to initiation into an organization or continued membership. Under that law and the federal Stop Campus Hazing Act, signed by President Joe Biden in 2024, Ohio State maintains a public list of hazing violations and penalties. It shows that so far this year, four fraternities, one sorority and one co-ed group have been sanctioned for hazing. Sigma Alpha Epsilon does not appear on the list for the last five years, though the student newspaper The Lantern said it has been sanctioned at least seven times since 2001. According to the newspaper’s archives, the chapter over the years has been found to have violated policies related to alcohol, hazing and endangering behavior, and at one point had its disciplinary probation extended for failing to comply with sanctions. Sigma Alpha Epsilon eliminated its “pledging” process for all its chapters nationwide in 2014 in part due to injuries and deaths. In 2022, 46 members of the SAE chapter at the University of New Hampshire were charged with hazing. Most agreed to perform community service and avoided conviction; the three who went to trial were acquitted because the judge said the state didn’t prove the acts were a “condition of initiation into, continued membership in or association with” the fraternity. Ramer reported from Concord, New Hampshire. Julie Carr-Smyth also contributed from Columbus.

Commentary: Abdul El-Sayed’s Michigan miracle
articles.description: The conventional wisdom is that Michigan Senate-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s midterms victory was unremarkable given that he “only” won by 7 points in a purple state, while Democrats won by 14 points nationwide, and “underperformed” Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson by 2 points. To the contrary, I believe that El-Sayed’s victory was both remarkable and historic given the […]
articles.content: Vote Abdul poster in Ann Arbor. August 2, 2026 | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceThe conventional wisdom is that Michigan Senate-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s midterms victory was unremarkable given that he “only” won by 7 points in a purple state, while Democrats won by 14 points nationwide, and “underperformed” Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson by 2 points. To the contrary, I believe that El-Sayed’s victory was both remarkable and historic given the unprecedented obstacles that he had to overcome to become the first Muslim ever elected to the U.S. Senate. El-Sayed had to survive a months-long, vile and dishonest, smear campaign orchestrated by a sitting president and echoed by his sycophants. President Trump sneeringly called Abdul a “communist,” a “terrorist sympathizer,” and/or “a jihadist lunatic who hates our country” in practically every speech and social media post over the last two months of the campaign. It was the most brutal and bigoted presidential assault on a political candidate in modern American history. His Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, never disavowed the naked bigotry, and claimed that El-Sayed “believes America deserved 9-11.” He repeatedly fabricated allegations about the Muslim Brotherhood, Hamas, and Hezbollah, and, at their last debate, showed how low he would go by asking “are you for America, or are you for these terrorists groups?” Trump invokes anti-Muslim rhetoric to attack El-Sayed at Michigan rally supporting Rogers, James To my knowledge, not a single national or Michigan Republican had the basic human decency to call for an end to the shameful lies and smears. El-Sayed also had to overcome an obscene amount of outside PAC spending by right-wing billionaires. In the August Democratic primary, AIPAC and corporate PACs spent over $60 million to defeat Abdul and support his primary opponent, Haley Stevens. This obliterated the all-time record for the most PAC money in a Democratic congressional primary. El-Sayed refuses corporate PAC money, and was outspent by about 10-to-1 in the primary despite outraising Stevens among individual donors. The PAC dollars were exclusively devoted to deceptive ads designed to impugn Abdul’s character. Tellingly, no major Democratic leaders objected to this attempt by right-wing PACs to buy a Democratic primary. In the general election, Rogers was supported by over $170 million of PAC spending (most from Elon Musk, AIPAC, and the MAGA PAC), about twice the outside spending for El-Sayed (all of which came from the Senate Democratic PAC and issue-oriented groups). Again, El-Sayed outraised Rogers from small donors, but was outspent by about 2-to-1. Another major challenge was that El-Sayed faced a state Democratic Party that was almost universally united behind his primary opponent, Haley Stevens. Governor Gretchen Whitmer, retiring Senator Gary Peters, Attorney General Dana Nessel, and ex-Senator Debbie Stabenow all endorsed Stevens, along with many other state and local party officials. To their credit, Senator Elissa Slotkin, Congresswoman Debbie Dingell, and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson chose to stay neutral and let voters decide. The weekend before general election day, Haley Stevens reneged on her earlier endorsement of El-Sayed and endorsed Mike Rogers. This backfired by finally coalescing the state party establishment behind Abdul. U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-South Carolina), center left, speaks during a press conference supporting U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, center right, on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026 at North End Church of God in Christ in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance) Finally, there was a double standard in mainstream media coverage of the Michigan Senate campaign. The media scrutinized and parsed not only every phrase that El-Sayed uttered over the last 20 years, but also statements by distant relatives with whom he never lived and twitch streamers who generate attention by being provocative. But the media did not apply the same level of scrutiny in pressing Mike Rogers to explain how he and his wife made millions of dollars after leaving Congress, why he flip-flopped to support election denialism, or why he employed a white supremacist as a campus organizer. The media obsessively parroted the Rogers’ campaign talking points that El-Sayed was struggling with both Jewish voters statewide and Black voters in Detroit. The debate within the Michigan Jewish community was in fact real and newsworthy, but the electoral relevance was greatly exaggerated given that Jews represent only about 1.5 percent of Michigan voters. While there are many more Black voters, the “concerns” turned out to be wishful thinking by the Rogers campaign as El-Sayed captured over 90 percent of the Black vote in Detroit. Yet the media barely reported on the incredible success of the El-Sayed campaign in shifting large numbers of young, unaffiliated, and Arab-American voters to his side which led to his comfortable victory margin. The simplistic claim that Abdul El-Sayed’s victory was much more expected than Democratic victories in, say, Mississippi or Texas, falls apart in view of the massive challenges that dwarfed those faced by any other Senator-elect in the country. He and his grassroots campaign met the moment, as did the decent people of Michigan, who rejected the presidential smears, the big money PACs, a hostile state party bureaucracy, and a biased mainstream media, to deliver one of the greatest political stories in Michigan, and American, history.

articles.title: Young, diverse voters showed up for midterms as older, Trump voters stayed home
articles.description: Much of the midterm “blue tsunami” came from diverse, enthusiastic young voters with financial struggles who flocked to the polls, and also Trump voters sitting out the election, according to two experts analyzing turnout in a handful of states with detailed results. The results, they say, could mean a mandate for bringing costs down and […]
articles.content: Sioux Falls residents vote in South Dakota's general election on Nov. 3.Turnout fell to a historic low in the state as Democrats gained in the Republican-dominated legislature. Democratic gains in many states could be explained more by the turnout gap than by voters switching their allegiance. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)Much of the midterm “blue tsunami” came from diverse, enthusiastic young voters with financial struggles who flocked to the polls, and also Trump voters sitting out the election, according to two experts analyzing turnout in a handful of states with detailed results. The results, they say, could mean a mandate for bringing costs down and more power for young Latinos, but also a danger for Democrats if Republicans rally back to the polls in 2028. “It looks like more Trump voters who didn’t vote Republican stayed home rather than switching (to Democrats),” said Lenny Bronner, founder of Broome Street Labs and a data scientist formerly with the Washington Post, based on his analysis of 13 states with detailed results. “Those voters are easier for the GOP to win back than those who chose a Democratic candidate,” Bronner said. Bronner estimated 75% of Democratic gains came from a turnout gap and about 20% from Republicans switching sides and voting for Democrats. His analysis included turnout data for Texas, Georgia, South Carolina, Colorado, New Mexico, Virginia, North Carolina, Arkansas, Iowa, Florida, West Virginia, Minnesota and Michigan. The share of Democrats’ gain that came from a turnout gap ranged from 40% for Texas to 133% for Michigan among the states he studied; some states had only partial detailed results. Bronner wrote on X (formerly Twitter) that partial results in Texas showed that voters flipped their ballots more than expected; 45% of Democratic gains there came from voters switching away from Republicans. “So far, Texas is the only state where our model indicates that persuasion explains more of Democrats net gain than turnout does!” he wrote. A University of Florida political science professor, Michael McDonald, also saw a turnout surge for young voters faced with high grocery bills, student loan debt and sluggish wages, based on detailed results from Georgia and Colorado. Trump’s older voter constituency was more likely to stay home, he wrote in a Substack post. In both Colorado and Georgia, 18- to 25-year-olds had the biggest jump in turnout compared with the 2022 midterms, he wrote, while it fell for voters older than 40. “This all makes sense when you realize that we just witnessed the most diverse electorate for a midterm election in U.S. history, with big increases over 2022 in Latino turnout,” McDonald wrote. “Latinos are markedly younger than whites, so if their turnout increases it means more younger voters are in the mix.” Even in Florida, where Republicans continued to dominate elections, GOP turnout was lower than in 2022 despite a registration drive that increased Republican registration by 400,000, McDonald wrote in another Substack post. Republican Gov. Rick DeSantis’ drive to purge voter rolls, affecting mostly Democratic and unaffiliated voters, may have played a role, he wrote. “DeSantis’ shrewd politics appears in part due to suppressing Democrat and unaffiliated votes through a massive voter registration purge that pushed Florida red, rather than rallying Florida Republicans to vote,” McDonald wrote. On a statewide basis, midterm turnout increased almost 13 points in Mississippi since the last midterms, as the state appears close to electing its first Black senator since Reconstruction. Turnout fell to a historic low in South Dakota, where Republicans still dominate voting. The University of Florida’s turnout calculations provide a window into overall turnout, which it measures as a share of voter-eligible population, excluding noncitizens and ineligible felons. McDonald did the calculations for the University of Florida’s Election Lab, and Stateline compared them to 2024 and 2022 turnouts for a state-by-state map. The analysis shows the highest turnout for 2026 in Maine, Minnesota and Michigan, all at more than 63%, and lowest in West Virginia (33.3%), Oklahoma (37.1%) and Hawaii, Indiana and Tennessee (all 38.2%). South Dakota’s midterm vote remained heavily Republican, though Democrats gained legislative seats for the first time in 18 years. They took four new seats, for a total of 12 in the 105-seat legislature. South Dakota had higher turnout in 2022, possibly in part because of contentious statewide ballot measures for Medicaid expansion, which passed, and marijuana legalization, which failed. articles.title: Data center restrictions pass in Saginaw Township and Romulus
articles.description: Two Michigan communities approved measures restricting data center development this week, joining a growing list of local governments that are hitting the brakes.
articles.content: (.shock - stock.adobe.com / 335703289)Two Michigan communities approved measures restricting data center development on Monday, joining a growing list of local governments which have done so.On Monday night, the Saginaw Township Board of Trustees voted to approve an ordinance regulating the development of data centers in the area.According to MLive, the 15-page ordinance lays out a number of standards any prospective data center must meet. Noise produced by data centers may not exceed 40 decibels at the property line, buildings and equipment must sit at least 500 feet from residential property, and cooling processes must use a closed-loop or recycled water system, among other regulations.Developers must notify any residents within half a mile of planned data center sites, and hold a minimum of two community meetings on any proposed developments. Medium and hyperscale data centers, as defined by the ordinance, are restricted to a narrow section of the township.The ordinance will go into effect on November 16.Things are moving slightly faster in Romulus, where the city council unanimously approved a 180-day moratorium on data centers, also on Monday night. It took effect immediately.The six-month pause on approval of any data center development will be used to craft permanent data center regulations for the city.Several residents present at Monday’s council meeting reportedly asked the city to ban data centers entirely, a sentiment echoed by two council members. Mayor Robert McCraight said any new city ordinances should consider the value smaller data centers may have to local industry.Neither locality has faced a data center planned for development yet, so both resolutions were passed as a preventive measure. And they are far from the only ones.A long list of local governments in Michigan have passed restrictions on data center development over the last year. A Michigan Public analysis in July found that as many as 52 local township and city governments across the state had passed data center moratoriums, though more have done so since.The state’s political environment seems set to grow even more opposed to data centers in the coming months.While Governor Gretchen Whitmer has generally been supportive of data centers, growing public backlash has led many Michigan politicians to adopt more skeptical stances.Notably, Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson has called for a statewide moratorium on data centers pending the development of regulations holding developers to certain environmental, energy, and public transparency standards.

articles.content: Oura announced its quarterly earnings today and said it agreed to acquire Counsel Health for $625 million, after adding the company’s AI chatbot to its app earlier this year. Counsel Health calls itself an “AI-native primary care company,” using the app to deliver AI-generated responses and insights based on users’ health data reported from their wearables that can then proceed to a conversation with one of its in-house physicians. Oura says it expects the deal to close before the end of the year. Oura CEO Tom Hale said in an interview with Bloomberg that the acquisition is part of a plan to connect wearables, clinical AI, and access to doctors based on insights from biometric data to answer questions or monitor ongoing conditions. Counsel Health’s AI chatbot can connect Oura users to a real doctor directly from the app and draw on users’ biometric data from their wearables in its answers to medical questions. The plan they describe in the press release is to focus on three areas, including preventative care, acute care for episodic health concerns, and specialty and chronic care for things like reproductive and cardiometabolic health. According to Bloomberg, Counsel Health’s CEO Muthu Alagappan says it’s also planning to expand its network of on-demand physicians, which is currently “made up of about 50 people.” Counsel’s 70 employees will join Oura as part of the deal, with Alagappan becoming Oura’s chief clinical AI officer. Oura says in its announcement that Counsel will also continue offering its medical AI platform outside of Oura’s user base through new and existing enterprise partners, including “health plans, health systems, consumer health organizations, and employers.”

articles.title: Transition underway in Flint as city elects new mayor
articles.description: Council member Tonya Burns defeated incumbent Mayor Sheldon Neeley in last week’s election
articles.content: Flint city hall will see many changes in the coming weeks.(Steve Carmody / Michigan Public)The transition at Flint City Hall is getting underway.Flint councilmember Tonya Burns defeated incumbent Mayor Sheldon Neeley last week in the 2026 election. She takes her oath of office on Nov. 24 and officially moves into the mayor's office Dec. 1.But first, the transition from one administration to another. Several top mayoral appointees, including the police and fire chiefs, have announced they are departing. On Tuesday, Neeley said his staff is ready to assist mayor-elect Burns with the transition.“We’ll be here,” Neeley told reporters. “We want the work to continue ... the work is much more important than any election.”Neeley said he hasn’t had much communication with Burns since the election, aside from a brief telephone conversation and an email exchange.Michigan Public was unable to reach Burns on Tuesday to ask her about the transition.At a news conference last week, Burns introduced members of her transition team and talked about the need to cultivate a working relationship with Flint’s newly elected city council members.

articles.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
articles.description: Researcher finds 35,000 Grok Build apps wide open to anyone who looked for them.
articles.content: Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows. The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it. You had one job Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals.Read full article Comments
