articles.title: How a 29-year-old flipped a state House seat in a West Michigan Republican stronghold
articles.description: Joseph McClusky will represent the 86th District of the Michigan State House after unseating Republican incumbent Nancy DeBoer in the midterms.
articles.content: Joseph McClusky is the newly elected state house representative for the 86th district. (Michelle Jokisch Polo / Michigan Public )The Holland region has elected a Democrat to serve in the 86th Michigan House district — a region that for decades has elected Republicans. The district includes Holland and portions of Allegan and Ottawa counties. Joseph McClusky, 29, managed to unseat 72-year-old Republican incumbent Nancy DeBoer in a close race. Speaking to Stateside Host April Baer on Monday, McClusky said he attributes his win to his campaign's willingness to go directly to voters. "We knocked on 70,000 doors, and a lot of people that we talked to had never had a Democrat step foot on their front porch (and) ask them what's on their mind," he said. "It opened the door a little bit to be able to talk about what a Democrat actually is and what the Democratic Party can be." Nearly a decade before running for the seat, McClusky most closely identified with the Republican Party. Growing up in a conservative family in Burton, he said the first thing he did when he started undergraduate school at Hope College in Holland was join the Hope Republican club. "I remember one of the nights at the Republican National Convention in Cleveland in 2016, as a guest of the Michigan Delegation, hearing people like Ted Cruz saying, 'Vote your conscience,' and being booed off stage," he said. "For a while, I thought I could still be in the party and just disagree with the head of the ticket, but what I saw at that convention was the party and the man becoming one."That year, Cruz, a U.S. Senator from Texas, challenged Donald Trump for the Republican presidential nomination, but Cruz's criticism of Trump and the growing support for Trump among Republican leaders at the time contributed to the end of his campaign.McClusky's affiliation with the Republican Party didn't happen overnight. He said as he sought more opportunities on campus and came out as gay, he realized he could no longer endorse the values of the Republican Party. "I still stay true to the values that I was raised with: to work hard, tell the truth, love my neighbor as myself," he said. "More often than not, those values are found more in the Democratic Party than the Republican Party." The freshman state representative campaigned on lowering the cost of gas and groceries, tailoring his message around his personal experience relying on government assistance during parts of his childhood. His dad was injured on the job, and his mom went from being a stay-at-home mom to working in his school cafeteria."I know what its like to be in a family that's one emergency, one injury or one setback away from the edge," he said. "And how important it is to have leaders who understand that the decision made in Lansing are not abstract but hey affect whether we can afford rent for groceries." On the campaign trail, McClusky also told voters about his experience renting. "My spouse and I are currently renting," he said. "We would love to own a home and we both work hard, we're both saving but it just feels out of reach and being to talk about my experiences resonated with with a lot of voters." Looking ahead, McClusky said he's hoping to focus on passing legislation that "gets government back on track, makes life more affordable and government more accountable.""Whether you voted for me or didn't vote for me, my job is to make sure that I'm doing everything I can to protect you from overzealous corporations, from an overreaching federal government, making sure that I'm bringing money and resources back to the district," he said. McClusky will be sworn in at the beginning of 2027. Full interview with Joseph McCluskyApril Baer: We've been talking a lot lately about elections and the size of the blue wave that swept over Michigan. One of the biggest surprises came in West Michigan's 86th District, where Democratic challenger Joseph McClusky, age 29, flipped a West Michigan state House seat in a region that for decades has elected Republicans. This district includes Holland and portions of Allegan and Ottawa counties. We've joined Joseph McClusky to talk to us today about his campaign and everything that came through it.Joseph, welcome to Stateside. It's good to have you.Joseph McClusky: Thank you. April, it's great to be here.Baer: Can you tell me a little bit about yourself? I know that back in college you went to Hope, which is the liberal arts college in West Michigan, and I think you were involved in campus Republicans while you were there, is that right?McClusky: It's true, it's true. I grew up on the east side of the state in Burton, Michigan, just outside of Flint, in a working class family. My dad was a radiology technician, and my mom stayed at home with me and my two older sisters, and later went on to work in the school cafeteria. Came out to West Michigan to go to Hope College, where I studied political science. And having grown up in a very conservative and Republican environment, the first thing I did when I got to campus was join the Hope Republicans.Baer: I read somewhere that you even attended the 2016 RNC when the Republicans were gathering in Cleveland. How did you end up sort of deciding that that wasn't for you and ultimately getting into Democratic politics?McClusky: I've always been a politics nerd and I enjoyed going to campaign rallies for both parties. But it was actually going to that convention and some of the conversations I had with friends as Donald Trump came onto the political scene, that I no longer saw those values that I was raised with in the Republican Party. I remember one of the nights at the Republican National Convention there in Cleveland in 2016, as a guest of the Michigan Delegation — hearing people like Ted Cruz saying, "Vote your conscience," and being booed off stage.For a while, I thought that I could still be in the party and just disagree with the the head of the ticket. But what I saw at that convention was the party and the man becoming one. And I thought to myself, if that's the direction that this party wants to go, it's one that it's a path of destruction and I don't need to be a part of it. Now, I didn't become a Democrat overnight. I went on a longer journey, had conversations, sought out more opportunities on campus through conversation. It's been a slower journey, but I still stay true to the values that I was raised with: to work hard, tell the truth, love my neighbor as myself, and more often than not, those values are found more in the Democratic Party than the Republican Party.Baer: So fast forward 10 years, it's 2026 and you're campaigning for state representative. You talked a lot on the trail about lower costs for gasoline and groceries. Were there things about your own experiences that you think resonated with voters you talked to?McClusky: I grew up in a working class family, and when I was in middle school, my dad was injured on the job. Our family realized firsthand what it means to need help and how important it is to have people stand with you in a hard moment, and we relied on government assistance to put food on the table and keep our family afloat. So I know what it's like to be in a family that's one emergency, one injury or one setback away from the edge.I know how important it is to have leaders who understand that the decisions made in Lansing are not abstract, but they affect whether we can afford rent for groceries or build a stable future for our families. Right now in our own community and across the state, too many families are doing everything right and still falling behind, and too many of our politicians are simply not showing up and meeting this moment. My spouse and I are currently renting. We would love to own a home. We both work hard, we're both saving, but it just feels out of reach, and being able to talk about not just my upbringing, but the experiences that my spouse and I are experiencing right now trying to own a home — I think resonated with a lot of people. Also when we talked to young people, we hear a lot from older politicians who talk about going back to a pre-Trump era. I'm not interested in having that conversation because so many of my peers don't know what a pre-Trump era is. So I have been more interested in coming together and sharing what we want to see. Let's dream about what we want to see for our future, and how can we come together and try to build that in the midst of all of this destruction. Baer: Joseph, you and your partner, Stephen Rumler, have been married since 2023, and I wonder if that is part of what you mean when you say you're not necessarily interested in going back? I mean, was was there a time when you thought that that being gay meant that you would not have a place in politics?McClusky: Certainly, there was a time when I thought that meant I wouldn't have a place in politics, wouldn't have a place in the church. My spouse Steven is a church musician, and there has been along with that political journey, also a faith journey as well. That's what's grounded me in this community. This is a strongly faith based community, and so I tell people: I'm not running to change Holland into something it's not, but to bring forward the Holland that we know to be true. Just like in my own story, it's similar to Holland's story that those values that we have do not need to be abandoned, but they can be expanded to include more people. So that's sort of the message that we've been carrying across the line. I've had so many people reach out to me since since our victory Tuesday night, people who grew up in Holland, who left and said: 'I'm never going back there,' who are now thinking about returning, or people who were thinking about leaving now say: 'Wait, maybe I have a spot in this community.' That's meant so much to me. Baer: This was not your first campaign. You were part of the campaign staff for Bryan Berghoef race for the 2nd Congressional District, which was not successful. You also managed Larry Jackson, who is also a Democrat, in his run for this district, the 86th. That was the year that Nancy DeBoer won. What did you want to be different in your campaign? Were there lessons, things that you learned in those earlier races that shaped the way you approached this one?McClusky: Certainly, the race with Bryan Berghoef, I think was most impactful because that was my first campaign. First exposure really to working in politics in the Holland area, and what I saw was a lot of people who cared about their neighbors, a lot of excitement, a lot of financial resources. I saw that a lot of those pieces were here, but I had not seen the kind of campaign that was able to pull all of those pieces together. So then in 2022, I did manage the race against Nancy DeBoer. At that time, I did not think that she was reflective of where the community was based on the mayoral election of 2019 that she lost. That gave me an opportunity to get to know a lot of folks in this community, a lot of the volunteers that I had worked with previously on the congressional race to continue working with them. So many of those volunteers that I got to know in 2019 and 2020 and 2022 were a core part of this campaign here in 2026. In 2024, I was the regional political director for the Michigan House Democratic Fund. So I worked with ten state House campaigns across West Michigan and as I heard other state reps talk about the programs they were fighting for the money that they were delivering for their district, I thought to myself, 'I've never heard my representative talk about what she's fighting for, talk about the money that she's delivering for the district.' What I took away from that was we need more representatives who are fighting for us, who are delivering results, and that's when I started to have the conversations of: 'Is it time for me to step out from behind the curtain and put my own name on the ballot?' And I'm so glad that I did.Baer: Joseph, the DeBoe

articles.title: OpenAI, Anthropic face new oversight as New York’s AI safety law takes effect
articles.description: New York is preparing to enforce its sweeping AI safety law, requiring major developers like OpenAI and Anthropic to register, disclose safety practices, and report critical incidents or face fines.
articles.content: New York is gearing up to enforce one of the country’s most significant AI safety laws. The state opened a registration portal Tuesday, with which large frontier AI developers like Anthropic and OpenAI will be required to register by January 1, 2027. The RAISE Act, New York’s safety and transparency bill, kicks in at the start of the year. It mandates that large frontier developers — companies with more than $500 million in annual revenue — have to publish safety frameworks on their websites, report critical safety incidents within 72 hours, and issue public model transparency reports. The newly formed Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust (DIGIT) will implement the RAISE Act and oversee large frontier AI labs. Penalties can be as high as $1 million for one violation and $3 million for subsequent violations. The state also can bring enforcement actions against companies that fail to register with the new portal, though a spokesperson declined to provide specifics. “Tech moguls tell us that their vision for AI is inevitable,” Governor Kathy Hochul said Tuesday during a press briefing. “They tell us get on board or get left behind… That any collateral damage is worth it as long as we win the race to the AI cliff.” On Tuesday, Hochul also launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research based at State University of New York’s Binghamton University. The center will independently evaluate the safety, security, and operation of advanced AI systems and work with DIGIT to review companies’ safety frameworks. Hochul first announced the center in January with $55 million in donations and capital. “We’re building a national model for smart, sensible AI regulation, a model that puts communities above corporations and people above powerful technology,” Hochul said. The RAISE Act isn’t the only safety law New York has passed. Last year, the state began enforcing a law that requires AI companion operators to regularly let users know they’re talking to a bot, and to make reasonable efforts to detect suicidal ideation and self-harm. In October, Hochul signed a separate chatbot safety law for minors, restricting behaviors like deceptive human-like interactions, emotionally manipulative or sycophantic responses, and encouragement of behaviors like suicide or disordered eating. That law takes effect June 1, 2027. Other states have also passed similar AI safety and transparency bills to the RAISE Act. California’s SB 53, which took effect in January, mandates that frontier AI labs have in place and publish safety frameworks, enact whistleblower protections, and report critical safety incidents within 15 days. Illinois’ SB 315, which will go into effect at the start of 2027, has similar requirements, plus includes independent safety compliance audits. Last year, the state began enforcing a law that requires AI companion operators to regularly let users know they’re talking to a bot, and to make reasonable efforts to detect suicidal ideation and self-harm. In October, Hochul signed a separate chatbot safety law for minors, restricting behaviors like deceptive human-like interactions, emotionally manipulative or sycophantic responses, and encouragement of behaviors like suicide or disordered eating. That law takes effect June 1, 2027. Other states have also passed similar AI safety and transparency bills to the RAISE Act. California’s SB 53, which took effect in January, mandates that frontier AI labs have in place and publish safety frameworks, enact whistleblower protections, and report critical safety incidents within 15 days. Illinois’ SB 315, which will go into effect at the start of 2027, has similar requirements, plus includes independent safety compliance audits. articles.title: Benzie County operations in doubt after voters defeat tax to pay bills
articles.description: For the second time this year, voters in the conservative enclave of northern Michigan rejected an operating millage that funds much of the county’s operations.
articles.content: Voters in Benzie County twice this year have rejected a tax that funds more than half the government’s operation The tax funds sheriff’s operations, parks and courts; it also funded the county’s townships The latest tax collection will carry the county through September, after that, a tax allocation board will decide what taxes the county can levy Police, parks and court operations may be at risk in Benzie County in northern Michigan after voters last week defeated a tax that funds most of its budget for the second time this year. Last week, the county southwest of Traverse City asked voters to approve for two years a 4.95-mill property tax that provides more than 60% of its budget. By a 54% to 46% margin, voters rejected the tax that would cost owners of a $200,000 home about $495 a year. A similar request lost by 12 votes in August. Without a voter-approved tax, state law requires the county to form a tax allocation board made up of county and other local officials to set a property tax rate for the county and its dozen townships without voter input. According to the Michigan Treasury, five of Michigan’s 83 counties use similar boards to set their tax rates. Interim County Administrator Leslie Bilbey said this week Benzie County has never had one. “We tried really hard to leave it in voters’ hands,” said Jon Willow, executive director of the Benzie Area Chamber of Commerce, which held town halls to encourage voters to support the tax. RELATED: EMS, jails, cannabis and more: How Michigan voted on local ballot issues Michigan election results: Governor, Senate, US House, proposals, more Here’s how Michigan voted on school millages, other tax increase proposals Voters approved two smaller countywide tax increases last week — one for animal control and another for drug enforcement — but Willow speculated that residents are hard hit by inflation and defeated the tax to save money. Voters in the county of 18,500 residents are older than the state as a whole, with nearly a third 65 or older, and also rejected an operating tax and sinking fund millage for the county’s schools last week. “It just looked like if it was on the ballot and it said tax or money, people just said no,” Willow said.Donate Statewide, voters approved most tax increases last week, including all but 14 of 124 public safety millage proposals, according to a Bridge Michigan analysis of data from Gongwer News Service. Support for school taxes statewide dipped slightly statewide to 59.5% of requests from 63.8% in May. Bilbey said the county has yet to ponder any cuts or layoffs and it’s too soon to tell what rate a tax allocation board might set. “That is uncharted territory for us right now,” Bilbey said. “We as a county won’t know what we will have for our general fund.” The tax expires next month but was last levied in July. Revenue from that collection should carry the county through its budget year, which ends Sept. 30, Bilbey said. This year, the tax generated about $6.4 million of the county’s $10.1 million general fund budget and generated nearly $1.2 million for the county’s dozen townships. “It hurts,” said Mark Roper, supervisor of the county’s Almira Township. Voters also rejected that township’s operating tax, meaning Roper’s board will be looking at steep cuts when it starts budget talks in January.

articles.title: US House Republicans elect Ohio firebrand Jim Jordan to lead party in next Congress
articles.description: WASHINGTON — U.S. House Republicans voted behind closed doors Tuesday to elect Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio as their leader after the party’s stunning losses in the midterm elections, the House Republican Conference announced. It was a 106-73 vote, according to a House Republican staff member. “Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight […]
articles.content: U.S. Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio speaks to members of the media as he arrives for a House Republican Conference meeting at the U.S. Capitol on Feb. 3, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)WASHINGTON — U.S. House Republicans voted behind closed doors Tuesday to elect Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio as their leader after the party’s stunning losses in the midterm elections, the House Republican Conference announced. It was a 106-73 vote, according to a House Republican staff member. “Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families,” Jordan told reporters after the GOP leadership elections. “When Democrats offer more government, we’ll offer more freedom. ” Jordan did not take questions. Jordan will succeed House Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana, who declined to run again. The incoming Republican minority leader will be charged with growing the party’s seats after the House GOP lost more than 40 after last week’s elections. Jordan will also be tasked with fundraising for his party, and negotiating with Democrats on must-pass legislation, such as appropriations bills. But with the smallest Republican House minority since the 1990s, the GOP will have little sway in a chamber dominated by the majority party. A handful of House races are still too close to call, but The Associated Press has called 166 seats for Republicans and 255 for Democrats for the incoming 120th Congress. Jordan, who has served in the House for two decades, chairs the House Judiciary Committee but has not held a senior GOP leadership position. Jordan is a staunch defender of President Donald Trump. He was a founder of the House Freedom Caucus of far-right GOP members. Jordan was up against Louisiana Republican Rep. Steve Scalise, the current Republican majority leader. Cheers could be heard outside the closed door meeting following the vote. Jordan and Scalise ran for speaker in 2023 after Republicans voted to strip then-Speaker Kevin McCarthy of his role. Scalise bowed out of that race before a House vote and Jordan failed to garner enough votes for the speaker’s gavel. Emmer, McClain reelected Republicans also reelected Minnesota’s Rep. Tom Emmer as GOP whip and Michigan’s Rep. Lisa McClain as conference chair, according to the House Republican Conference. McClain said the priority for Republicans in the next Congress would be to “earn back the trust of the American people and take back this House.” Republicans tapped Georgia’s Rep. Brian Jack for the National Republican Congressional Committee, the conference’s campaign arm, according to the conference. Senate Republicans also voted behind closed doors Tuesday to keep South Dakota Sen. John Thune as GOP leader. Senate Republicans will also be in the minority in January. Senate Democrats will hold at least 54, and as many as 56, seats. Democratic candidates Mary Peltola in Alaska and Scott Colom in Mississippi are leading in races that AP still has not called.

articles.title: What happens to mathematics when AI becomes an oracle?
articles.description: Mathematician Steven Strogatz discusses his new book, Big Math: The Hidden Codes That Run Our World.
articles.content: Our modern world runs on math, from social media algorithms, package delivery, and weather prediction to medical imaging and machine learning. The rise of computers helped fuel its dominance, enabling us to work with increasingly large numbers that would otherwise be beyond the capacity of our finite human brains. But with the rise of large language models, AI chatbots, and, soon, quantum computing, so-called "big math" is beginning to outstrip its creators entirely. What that means, and how we might adapt, is the focus of a new book, Big Math: The Hidden Codes That Run Our World, by applied mathematicians Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend. Strogatz is perhaps best known in his field for his co-authorship of a seminal 1998 paper with Duncan Watts on the collective dynamics of small-world networks. He has also studied chaos theory as applied to physics, the geometry of supercoiled DNA, and the biological collective oscillators, such as swarms of synchronously flashing fireflies and crickets that chirp in unison. In 2005, Strogatz extended his study of synchronicity to the crowds that caused the wobbling of London's Millennium Bridge. An award-winning communicator, Strogatz wrote three series of columns on mathematics for The New York Times in 2010, 2012, and 2025 and hosted a podcast for Quanta magazine from 2020–2021. He has written four popular books: Sync (2003), The Calculus of Friendship (2009), The Joy of X (2012), and the New York Times bestseller Infinite Powers (2019).Read full article Comments

articles.title: Report: Funding, opportunity gaps hurting educational progress in Michigan
articles.description: At an event in Detroit Tuesday morning, EdTrust-Midwest shared many concerning metrics about Michigan schools. Leaders say the state must invest deeply into districts with high concentrations of poverty and lean into literacy reforms to see change.
articles.content: An education advocacy and research group is calling for more funding for districts with high student poverty Incoming Senate Majority Leader Darrin Camilleri says this type of funding is a priority EdTrust-Midwest says money alone will not improve schools Michigan urgently needs to accelerate its progress in education, but it also must level the playing field so that students of all backgrounds can benefit, an advocacy and research group warned Tuesday. In its latest “State of Michigan Education Report.” EdTrust-Midwest is pushing for the state to direct more money to districts with the highest concentration of students living in poverty. It also called for continued investments in teacher training and literary curricula for students and bolstering the teacher and counselor workforce. “Over the past several years, state leaders have increased investments in public education, strengthened literacy policy, expanded college affordability, and invested in student supports,” the report says. “Yet student outcomes remain uneven, post-pandemic academic recovery is slow, and longstanding disparities in educational opportunity still persist.”The group unveiled its recommendations at an event in Detroit Tuesday morning. The report, titled ”Going for Gold: Setting the Standard for Michigan Achievement,” comes at a pivotal time for the state as a new administration prepares to take office and Michigan students continue to struggle academically. Only 38.9% of third graders are proficient in reading on state tests, more than a fourth of students are chronically absent and only about 55% of high school graduates attend college within six months of graduating, according to preliminary data. Related: Now, the hard part: Jocelyn Benson has big plans. Michigan has big problems To fix Michigan schools, experts urge better reading skills, less politics Just 1 in 4 Michigan juniors are ‘college ready,’ SAT scores indicate As Michigan forges forward on literacy, many ask: What about math? Michigan must focus literacy efforts on older students, too, experts say Jocelyn Benson education plan: Up teacher pay, tackle absenteeism, change constitution Brian L. Love, state director of EdTrust-Midwest, told Bridge he is concerned about several education metrics. Brian L. Love, state director of EdTrust-Midwest, speaks to an audience in Detroit about Michigan education. Love told Bridge Michigan groups and leaders should work together to improve public schools. (Photo courtesy of Eric Hobson via EdTrust-Midwest) “We can focus on a few things here and a few things there, and actually that’s probably been our state’s history, right? So the way we fix this now and soon is to tackle it all at the same time but we have to do it all together.” The group is calling for a stronger emphasis on helping high schoolers understand they can take advanced courses and college classes in high school. Building a stronger talent pipeline is “essential to Michigan’s economic competitiveness,” the report says. “The state’s postsecondary goals cannot be achieved only through making college more affordable if too many students never have an equitable opportunity to prepare for and successfully make the transition to college in the first place.” Funding needs EdTrust-Midwest is also calling for more transparency in how money dedicated for education is spent. Donate “Michigan’s next challenge is not simply to have an equitable funding formula on paper — it is to fully fund it, ensure dollars reach the students for whom they are intended, and make that investment visible to the public,” the report says. EdTrust-Midwest has advocated for the state to increase funding for districts with high concentrations of student poverty. These weighted funds for at-risk students are also known as the “opportunity index.” The state began including opportunity index funds in the school budget in 2023, during the last Democratic trifecta, when the party controlled the governor’s office and both legislative chambers. Among those championing the move was State Sen. Darrin Camilleri, now the incoming Senate majority leader. At Tuesday’s event in Detroit, where he received a “Champions of Hope” award from EdTrust-Midwest, Camilleri acknowledged a “big need” to provide more opportunity index funding. EdTrust-Midwest says the state is underfunding the opportunity index. It estimates full funding would take another $1.3 billion. “It’s been my north star: is how we can continue to fund this program to the best of our ability,” Camilleri said. “I think that we will find new resources to do that. Whether that happens in one budget cycle or four, remains to be seen. But I think it’s really important that we do invest more money in the opportunity index and get to as close to fully funded as humanly possible.” He estimates that savings from the state retirement system down the road could unlock about $3 billion more for schools. Still he said other education priorities including expanding child care and pre-K, providing higher teacher pay and improved special education take money. “We have some big challenges and so, there will, I’m sure, need to be a conversation about how we can actually pay for those things.” Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson has said she wants to improve public schools. She will need to work with a Democratic-dominated Michigan House and Senate. Meanwhile, some student trends are improving. The state reached a new high record with 84% of students graduating within four years. In addition, new grants are available to expand access to career and technical education courses and the state will start reimbursing high-poverty districts to provide dual enrollment courses to students. “We are really trying to get across the point that public schools are a powerful public good,” said Jennifer Mrozowski, senior director, strategic communications and external relations at EdTrust-Midwest. “We know that leading states have shown that there are wonderful things that can be done when you have all forces working together.”

articles.content: Google has announced a "super network" upgrade for its Fi cell service. For the past few years, Google Fi has operated exclusively on the T-Mobile network, but now it's adding support for a second 5G network. Oddly, Google refuses to say which one. Google's MVNO (mobile virtual network operator) launched in 2015 as Project Fi with support for both T-Mobile and Sprint service. The service initially only worked on Google's Nexus phones, which would switch between networks based on signal strength. After T-Mobile absorbed Sprint, Fi switched to being a single-network service in the US while continuing to hop between networks for international travel. With the super network, Google Fi is again a dual-carrier service stateside. Phones connected to Fi will be able to hop between T-Mobile 5G and a different 5G network to provide the best possible connectivity. articles.title: A Michigan Court of Appeals ruling gives Detroit Tenants Union new hope
articles.description: A new ruling by the Michigan Court of Appeals says landlords cannot evict tenants if their property does not have a certificate of compliance. The post A Michigan Court of Appeals ruling gives Detroit Tenants Union new hope appeared first on WDET 101.9 FM.
articles.content: A new ruling by the Michigan Court of Appeals says landlords cannot evict tenants if their property does not have a certificate of compliance. A Michigan Court of Appeals ruling is giving the Detroit Tenants Union some hope in its case against the 36th District Court. In July, the Tenants Union sued the court arguing it was allowing landlord’s to illegally collect rent with properties that were not up to city code. In September, a Wayne County judge dismissed the case saying its not the court’s job to verify the condition of a rental property. Now the Michigan Court of Appeals has ruled that landlords cannot evict tenants for unpaid rent if the property lacks a city-issued certificate of compliance. The tenants union’s lawyer is Donovan McCarty. He says this new ruling undercuts arguments made by 36th District court officials and gives his group a strong argument for re-instating the lawsuit. “The court made very clear that these certificates of compliance are incredibly important documents, things that landlords… cannot operate without,” McCarty says. “The new ruling in Skidmore v. Hayashi really undercuts many of the legal arguments that the 36th District court raised an opposition to our superintendent control complaint, and those same arguments that the court relied on in dismissing our complaint.” McCarty also notes that the union has already filed an appeal of the earlier dismissal.

articles.title: Oura to acquire AI-native primary care startup Counsel Health for $625M
articles.description: The deal comes a few weeks after Oura postponed its up to $2.2 billion IPO indefinitely, citing “uncertainty in the IPO market.”
articles.content: Oura announced on Tuesday that it’s acquiring AI-native primary care company Counsel Health for $625 million. The deal comes a few weeks after Oura postponed its up to $2.2 billion IPO indefinitely, citing “uncertainty in the IPO market.” Counsel Health is an AI-powered healthcare platform that combines a chat-based medical experience with access to licensed physicians. Its service was integrated into the Oura app in June. Users can connect with Counsel’s medical AI to get personalized medical advice, and chat with a physician when needed, all within the Oura app. Now, the companies plan to expand on their existing partnership to build across preventative care, acute care, and specialty and chronic care. While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals like RingConn and Ultrahuman are emerging to dethrone it, putting pressure on the company to keep innovating. By acquiring Counsel Health, Oura is looking to expand its business and help users access medical care. “Oura helps members understand their physiology and, with Counsel, they can take action on their health across a range of needs, from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care, and referrals,” said Oura CEO Tom Hale in a press release. Counsel Health raised a $25 million Series A a year ago, led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and GV. PitchBook estimates it had raised a total of $36 million. Following the acquisition, Oura says Counsel will continue serving existing and new enterprise partners, with the goal of expanding its AI-native care model to more people beyond Oura’s membership. Counsel CEO Muthu Alagappan will join Oura as chief clinical AI officer, alongside the company’s 70 employees, Bloomberg reports. “At Counsel, we’ve built medical AI around trust, safety and responsibility, keeping physicians in the loop for clinical decisions,” Alagappan said in the press release. “Oura’s data gives clinicians objective context, trended biometrics, and member engagement to deliver more informed care. From the start, our teams bonded over a joint vision, shared culture, and mission, further solidifying as we negotiated our deal over the past few months.” The deal is expected to close before the end of 2027. Oura also announced that its revenue grew 153% year-over-year to $533 million for the quarter ended on September 30. For its fiscal year 2026, Oura generated revenue of approximately $1.75 billion, marking 92% year-over-year growth. articles.title: 5 Michigan cities voted to create ‘health action’ boards. Now what?
articles.description: After a nearly $3 million campaign fueled by dark-money groups, voters in five Michigan cities created new committees to study healthcare costs and recommend policy changes. There are many unknowns.
articles.content: Five Michigan cities are now required to study healthcare costs after voters approved local charter amendments New ‘health action’ will be required to provide first recommendations to each city in less than two years The effort was driven by a ‘dark money’ nonprofit that featured anti-Republican messaging prominently in ads LANSING — Amid growing concerns over medical costs, voters in five Michigan cities last week approved measures to create new citizen-led boards that will recommend ways to lower costs and improve healthcare policies. How the boards will function is not clear, nor is the source of funding for the successful ballot campaigns. Liberal “dark money” groups spent nearly $3 million on the initiatives, which were spread across two toss-up congressional districts represented by Republicans who lost their reelection bids. But with healthcare costs top of mind for many, voters agreed to establish “citizens’ advisory health action” committees by wide margins in Benton Harbor (80% approval), Lansing (66% approval), East Lansing (69% approval), Kalamazoo (69% approval) and Portage (55% approval). Related: Mystery group circulates health petitions — and attacks Republicans Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan propels ‘Medicare for All’ debate Medical debts, anger soar as hospitals spend billions on expansions Now, it’s up to local governments in those cities to set up the boards, prompting fears of additional costs and uncertain outcomes. “If the voters want it, then we’ll set up a committee and we’ll do it,” Lansing Mayor Andy Schor told Bridge Michigan ahead of the election, expressing ambivalence and acknowledging the proposals made a political point. The cities will be limited in how much they can impact a sprawling national healthcare system with mind-numbing complexities, often opaque financing and Medicaid eligibility changes that are expected to reduce coverage and cost providers millions of dollars. But the new committees will be able to advise officials whose policies could support local health providers in ways that drive down costs, said Ryan Cohn, a spokesperson for City Action Michigan, the nonprofit driving the effort. “Voters sent a clear message,” said Cohn, who works for a Florida-based public relations firm, Sachs Media. “They want action on healthcare costs, and they’re done waiting for Congress to deliver it.” A late-October poll of Michigan voters showed high costs were a top concern, with health insurance or medical costs the primary driver. Donate Local amendments, local concerns The local proposals amended city charters to create seven- or eight-member committees to: Hold public forums to hear firsthand accounts from community members about how healthcare costs affect them Hold public forums to learn more about the role of federal and state policies in determining healthcare costs Track federal and state officials’ votes on healthcare legislation Prepare a “Healthcare Action Plan” for city leaders by Oct. 1 of each even-numbered year City councils then must hold public hearings by Oct. 15 of the same year for public discussion on the action plan. Advisory committee members will not be paid for their efforts, but must have necessary “research, analytical and community engagement skills,” according to the new rules. Some local officials have called the effort misguided. In October, the Kalamazoo City Commission passed a resolution unanimously opposing the local ballot measure. In public meetings, Mayor David Anderson expressed concerns about the ongoing financial burden organizing and running health advisory committees might impose on taxpayers. “Who’s gonna pay for all this work going forward in perpetuity? City residents,” Anderson said. “The cost of this will end up being a reduction in resources for something else that we might care a lot about.” Kalamazoo Commissioner Chris Praedel criticized the use of dark money to push the proposal, warning that it was “critically important for the public to think through how this sets a precedent or how this could impact things in a very dark, mischievous way.” It’s unclear how much the initiative will cost cities going forward. Committee members aren’t paid, although they can be compensated for costs, according to ballot language. “I would not envision it would be a lot,” said Alex Little, city manager in Benton Harbor. Political impact The proposals were notable for the way that they intertwined policy and electoral advocacy — the amendments were only proposed in largely Democratic cities within battleground congressional districts — and campaign advertising prominently attacked the Republican incumbents. Those lawmakers, US Reps. Tom Barrett and Bill Huizenga, were both unseated in close races in the Nov. 3 election. Democrats Will Lawrence and Sean McCann will replace them in Congress, respectively. Critics suggested the petition drives used to put the proposals on local ballots were designed to collect voter data and spread negative information about the incumbents. Community Action Lansing flyers and website targeted Republican US Rep. Tom Barrett. (Screenshot) In an election where Democrats saw sweeping gains, approval rates for the ballot proposals in the five liberal-leaning cities generally lagged behind support for major Democratic candidates like Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson. Chokwe Pitchford, a Berrien County commissioner whose nonprofit was paid by City Action Michigan to build support for the proposals, dismissed concerns that the initiative could set a precedent where municipal government itself becomes a platform for political advocacy. “Everyone has access to these tools, and if the other side wants to push a ballot proposal about the Second Amendment or about pro-life policies — if the voters vote for it, that’s democracy,” Pitchford said in an interview. The only representative of the City Action Michigan (formerly Community Action Michigan) that the campaign had not reported paying as of mid-October, Texas Charter Township trustee Barb Hammond, declined repeated requests for an interview with Bridge. What’s next? Local officials are now attempting to figure out how the new committees will work and what their responsibilities are. Municipal advisory boards or committees tend to focus on specific city operations like parks, libraries or transit systems, said Little, the Benton Harbor city manager. But “this is more of a study group to understand price and services for healthcare,” he said. Benton Harbor faces another challenge, he said: The city’s hospital closed 40 years ago, and the city — one where the median income is just above $31,000 and among the lowest in the state — may not have enough residents with healthcare and financing backgrounds to serve on the board. Moreover, he and others said it might seem like local governments can do little to shape healthcare policy. Benton Harbor’s public health initiatives are run through the county health department, for example. And decisions in a national healthcare system with its “infinite complexity” are mostly guided by federal and state policy, said Scott Greer, a University of Michigan professor who researches the ways in which political systems operate and shape health policy decisions. Still, the biennial reports that the committees produce will force “hyper-local” conversations that otherwise might not happen, Greer said. A community might explore how much emergency care is provided to homeless people, and therefore shift policy to extend more routine care to the homeless as a way to keep chronic conditions in check, Greer suggested as an example. That could be a cost saving for the system as those patients then rely less on expensive emergency room care. Benton Harbor, meanwhile, is facing hundreds of thousands of dollars in extra costs to pay for ambulance services because so many local patients are uninsured, said Little, the city manager. Perhaps an advisory committee focused on healthcare can find a solution, he mused. Cohn, at City Action Michigan, said the advisory committees can also offer collective voices that can reach Lansing. Pitchford, in Berrien County, argued the reports can be tailored to “the preconditions of your community.” “You might have an infant mortality crisis, you may have an obesity crisis, you may have pollution in the water, pollution in the air,” he said. “How do we gather all of that information, put it into something that is actionable, and take that to Lansing and to Washington, (DC) so that citizens can lobby their government on behalf of the changes to healthcare that they believe in?” Spokespersons for East Lansing and Portage said city officials now will review next steps. The money Through mid-October, the ballot committee for City Action Michigan reported receiving $2.8 million in donations, exclusively from dark-money nonprofits from outside Michigan not required to disclose their donors. They include American Opportunity Action, Cityscope, Global Impact Social Welfare Fund and Global Impact Ventures — all of which have been known to channel funding to liberal political initiatives while masking donor identities. Much of the funding was spent on ads supporting the proposals and to pay canvassers who collected signatures to get the initiatives onto local ballots. City Action Michigan also disclosed giving $100,000 to Pitchford’s 501(c)(4) nonprofit, Berrien Forward. Pitchford said the money, reported as a grant, was used to pay 17 canvassers to promote the proposals in Benton Harbor and Kalamazoo. “These were older Black women from churches, young people who were getting involved with the election process for the first time, who got trained on knocking doors, and we used that funding to invest in the election,” he said. It’s a “fair criticism” to note that neither he nor the voters know where the money came from, Pitchford acknowledged. He said he makes “value-based assessments” when groups approach him to work on their issues. “No funder, no group has ever asked me to do anything that I don’t believe in,” Pitchford added.

articles.content: U.S. Customs station at the Blue Water Bridge in Port Huron, Michigan. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)Gov. Gretchen Whitmer is using her final months in office to attack food tariffs imposed by the administration of President Donald Trump. On Tuesday, Whitmer called for the U.S. Department of Treasury to end its tariffs imposed on food products, while also requesting that the federal government reimburse Michigan residents for the increased costs they’ve incurred from the tariff regime. Whitmer, in a letter to U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, noted that Trump’s federal tariff policies have had a disproportionate effect on Michigan families. She also pointed out that, according to the National Taxpayers Union Foundation, Michigan households have faced an average tariff burden of $6,485 per household since January 2025. Whitmer’s office said that burden was the highest in the country. Meanwhile, food prices have continued to rise, Whitmer wrote, and grocery prices have increased by 2.4% in 2025. “Right now, Michigan families are paying the highest tariff burden in the nation because of DC Republicans’ agenda, and those costs are showing up every time they check out at the grocery store,” Whitmer wrote. “In Michigan, we’ve worked hard to put money back in people’s pockets, but we need a federal trade policy that works with our allies, brings supply chains home, and makes life more affordable. Families deserve relief from rising prices on the essentials they depend on every day.” Whitmer signs executive order to examine impact of Trump tariffs on Michigan’s economy The letter also emphasized how the tariff regime has heavily damaged the U.S. relationship with Canada. “Specifically, exports to Canada fell 12.3% last year, signaling severe strain with our strongest trading partner — these tariffs and sudden policy reversals have weakened Michigan’s competitiveness and disrupted long‑standing trade relationships,” Whitmer wrote. “Federal leaders can step up and make real change. I ask that you end the new food tariffs this administration has levied in 2025 and 2026, and reimburse Michiganders for the increased cost of food.” When asked for comment by Michigan Advance, a Treasury Department spokesperson pointed to comments Bessent made last month on NBC’s Meet The Press. “If you look underneath the hood of the numbers, core inflation has been very flat. Before this month, it had been down for four months in a row,” Bessent said. “So core inflation is down. Food is below the Fed’s targets. Prescription drugs have had the biggest decrease in history. Rents are down. So this is an energy shock. We will get to the other side of the Iran conflict, and those prices will come down.” 5:02 pmThis story has been updated with comments from Treasury Secretary Bessent.

articles.title: Regional transit agency supports Sterling Heights’ proposal for passenger-rail study
articles.content: The public agency that oversees mass transit in Southeast Michigan says it’s supportive of Sterling Height’s plan to explore the addition of using existing railroad tracks for freight for passenger service as well. Sterling Heights city officials recently announced in a press release they are initiating an effort to look into turning the Contrail north-south freight line in Warren and Sterling Heights, now used to transport auto and other industrial parts and equipment, into part of a “broader passenger rail network” to connect county residents to jobs, downtown sports and entertainment, and destinations currently served by Amtrak. City officials said they anticipate preliminary discussions among officials with the cities of Warren and Detroit, as well as Macomb County, Conrail, the Michigan Department of Transportation, the Regional Transit Authority of Southeast Michigan, SMART, Amtrak and other stakeholders. Ben Stupka, RTA executive director, said in a statement Tuesday: “When a community steps up for better transit, it helps build a stronger, more connected region. We appreciate Sterling Heights for planning ahead and inviting regional partners to join the discussion early. Working together on ideas like this is important, and the RTA is always happy to join those conversations.” Macomb County Executive Mark Hackel declined to comment on the proposal last week. Sterling Heights city employee Nahro Matti, on the direction of the City Council, last week presented a “white paper” to the council on the issue. “Preserving this corridor keeps an important transportation option available for our residents and the region,” City Manager Mark Vanderpool said in a press release. “We are beginning a regional conversation about whether this existing asset could support future passenger rail service and meet Sterling Heights and the surrounding area’s long-term transportation needs. While we are not committing to a rail project today, we recognize that losing portions of the corridor would make that opportunity much more difficult to pursue.” Potential station areas identified include stops in Sterling Heights near M-59 (Hall Road), and near the General Motors Technical Center between Mound Road and Van Dyke and 12 and 13 mile roads in Warren. “These areas would require further evaluation, along with possible connections to downtown Detroit, the airport and existing passenger rail service,” the release says. “The concept remains in the early stages. No passenger rail project, station locations, funding commitments or construction schedule have been approved. Any next steps would require additional review and coordination with regional partners.” The primary aim of the proposal is to connect Macomb County to “the wider passenger rail system serving Detroit, Ann Arbor, Kalamazoo, Chicago, and other destinations,” Matti says in the white paper. It could also connect other destinations, such as Detroit Metro Airport in Romulus. Matti says rail proponents need to take advantage of the existing Conrail line, noting that the company recently removed track from the line north of Hall Road in Shelby Township. “If more segments are removed like portions north of about 22 Mile Road that appear to already be gone, the region could lose a rare north-south rail corridor that would be very difficult to rebuild later,” he says. “The key recommendation is that the remaining corridor should be preserved and studied before any additional rail segments are removed.” The new service could provide pickups and dropoffs once per hour at the locations. “The line would support downtown sports and entertainment travel, and it could also help with airport-oriented trips to DTW,” Matti says. “However, the larger purpose would be to give Macomb County residents a practical connection to the existing rail network, especially for trips to Chicago and other cities that are already served by Amtrak.” Amtrak’s existing service consists of a line that it says connects Port Huron and Detroit with Pontiac, East Lansing, Grand Rapids and Chicago. “Enjoy simple online booking, quick check-ins, roomy seating, free Wi-Fi and beautiful scenery as you ride along the rails,” Amtrak says in promoting the service. Matti points out that Warren and Sterling Heights are the third and fourth largest cities in the state, “yet neither city has direct passenger rail access.” “Smaller Michigan communities such as Albion, which has a population of 7,700, are already connected to the Amtrak network,” he says. “This does not mean smaller communities should lose service. Rather, it shows that two of Michigan’s largest cities should be studied seriously for future rail access.” Conversations among the stakeholder “would help determine regional interest and potential support for a professional feasibility study,” Matti says. “A study would evaluate passenger demand, track conditions, coordination with freight operations, station locations, safety, costs and funding options. Public input would also be part of evaluating any future passenger rail proposal.” The RTA was established by state law in 2012 to plan, fund, coordinate and accelerate “regional transit services, projects and programs” in Macomb, Oakland, Wayne and Washtenaw counties, RTA says on its LinkedIn page. “RTA is responsible for leading regional planning, developing and implementing new services, allocating federal and state funding to transit service operators, and securing new regional funding sources for public transit,” it says. Matti says he consulted with former assistant manager Jeffrey Bahorski, current Assistant Manager Dale Dwojakowski, Councilman Michael Radtke Jr., city Planner Ryan Fox, and city Development Manager Jake Parcell before penning the paper.

Winter is coming. Can Democrats succeed in chilling soaring energy prices?
articles.description: WASHINGTON — Democrats during the midterm election campaign promised bold steps to make life more affordable if voters elected them to control Congress next year. They won, in a historic blue wave that’s already given them comfortable majorities in both the House and Senate. But Democrats likely will find that bringing down gasoline and other energy […]
articles.content: Democrats who won control of Congress are likely to find that bringing down gasoline and other energy prices in time for winter is largely a process out of their control. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)WASHINGTON — Democrats during the midterm election campaign promised bold steps to make life more affordable if voters elected them to control Congress next year. They won, in a historic blue wave that’s already given them comfortable majorities in both the House and Senate. But Democrats likely will find that bringing down gasoline and other energy prices as winter arrives will take more than an act or two of Congress. And it’s largely a process out of their control. “You can’t legislate your way out of high gasoline prices,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, which tracks prices. Since the United States attacked Iran on Feb. 28, fuel prices have soared. A gallon of regular gasoline averaged $3.98 Tuesday, AAA reported. While that’s down from recent weeks, it’s still well above the $3.07 of a year ago. Diesel prices Tuesday averaged $6.16 a gallon, ballooning from $3.73 a year ago. Home heating oil averaged a staggering $6.14 a gallon last week, up from $3.62 a year ago, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Electricity costs were up 3.8% and natural gas was up 4.4% over the 12 months ending in September, said the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics. Republicans will control Congress during the rest of this year’s session, and Democrats will be in charge beginning in January. Regardless of who has the majority, the government’s ability to bring consumer energy prices down over the short term is limited. Some Democrats are already blunt about what they can do about prices. “I’m not telling people I’m going to be able to lower X by X number of cents, but I’m telling them they’re going to have somebody who’s going to fight like hell for them,” Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, who’s in line to chair the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee next year, told reporters at the Capitol Monday. There are quick fixes. They can involve suspending fuel taxes, drawing from petroleum reserves and easing restrictions on certain products. Most of those strategies have been tried this year, and have had minimal if any impact. Lowering fuel taxes “The most obvious quick fix would be to eliminate the federal gas tax,” said Jeff Lenard, a vice president of the National Association of Convenience Stores, a trade group. He saw little else Congress could do quickly but added “if the federal tax is eliminated, that would create a budget hole elsewhere for the federal government,” and ending the gas tax would address only about 5% of the current cost of fuel. Gas and diesel prices in Forest Glen, Maryland, on Oct. 5, 2026. (Photo by Jane Norman/States Newsroom) Proposals to suspend the 18.4-cents-a-gallon federal gasoline tax and the 24.4-cents-a-gallon tax on diesel fuel have been a popular, easily understandable way of trying to get prices down quickly. Members of Congress from both parties have been trying this year to push the legislation. Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., wants a 90-day suspension. Rep. Jeff Van Drew, R-N.J., wants an 18-month tax holiday and a phase-in of the full tax when that period ends. Rep. Brendan Boyle, D-Pa., has called for suspending the tax when the national average price of gasoline tops $4 a gallon. But, said the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service last month, suspension of the federal tax “may not reduce consumer prices at all. Gasoline suppliers, distributors, refiners, and blenders could choose to reduce prices by more or less than 18.4 cents per gallon or, in theory, not reduce prices at all.” While no legislation to curb federal taxes has been approved, fuel tax holidays have been tried in different states. Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, North Carolina, Ohio, and Utah are suspending gas taxes or delaying increases this year. Washington’s Tax Foundation found California’s taxes and fees are the nation’s highest at 73.6 cents a gallon, followed by Illinois at 70.4 cents. The lowest taxes and fees are in Alaska at 9 cents a gallon. The emergency supply One big strategy for keeping price and supply stable was supposed to be the nation’s Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Created in 1975 after the price and supply shocks of the previous two years, the oil filled underground salt caverns along the Gulf Coast in Texas and Louisiana. Fifteen years ago, the reserve had about 726 million barrels. At the end of October, the supply was down to 282 million barrels, its lowest level in 44 years. President Donald Trump authorized the release of millions of barrels of oil during the Iran war, and President Joe Biden ordered major drawdowns to counter supply disruptions after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. This year, the supply from the U.S. and other nations, as well as lower consumer demand because of higher prices, helped ease the economic pain, said an analysis from Washington’s Bipartisan Policy Center. But, it added, “The events of the last few months have also demonstrated the limitations of the SPR. The reserve’s lower stock levels in the run-up to the Iran conflict limited the volumes available for release.” What can the government do? Trump last month eased restrictions on dyed diesel, often called red diesel, widely used in agriculture, and made a deal to bring more diesel from Russia into world markets. None of these strategies, though, is likely to make a lot of difference to consumers. “You can pull small levers, but the president has pulled most of those levers,” said De Haan. The most powerful players in regulating electricity rates and home heating oil are largely state and local agencies. But, said Charles Hua, founder and executive director of PowerLines, a nonpartisan consumer education organization, “federal policymakers including Congress and the president can still have an impact over utility bills.” He cited the ability to pass “policies that can modernize grid planning and utility business models, using their platform to elevate these issues, and engaging with state and regional actors on grid decisions that can impact utility bills.” The Iran war Trump could take what’s arguably the fastest way to provide relief to consumers from the high oil prices this winter by reaching an agreement to end the war with Iran. Prior to the war, roughly 20% of the world’s oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow passageway between Oman and Iran. The strait has been closed, or the site of attacks, since the war began. Here’s where the new Democratic-run Congress could have influence: It can pressure the administration to end the war. Serious talks are underway among Democratic leaders as to whether, or when, to cut off or at least severely limit war funding, perhaps during the lame-duck session now underway. “Will everything pass? Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump’s and Republicans’ intransigence, of course not,” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer of New York told a forum at the progressive Center for American Progress last week. “And let’s not forget one of our most powerful tools: Democrats have power on spending bills that require our votes, and we should use it. No more funding for a forever war with Iran,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, told the 2026 Popular Mandate conference on Tuesday, a gathering of progressives. Even an end to the war is no guarantee of sharply lower prices. Oil is a globally traded commodity, its supply and price affected by all sorts of developments. In 2022, prices spiked to levels similar to and even higher than the current costs after the Russian invasion of Ukraine disrupted world markets that were concerned about losing Russian oil. That war continues, meaning tensions in the Middle East are likely to go on, raising questions about the security of Saudi Arabia’s oil fields. De Haan, like most analysts, is wary of any fast solution. Oil prices are affected by too many different developments. “There’s a lot of different things going on at the same time,” he said. “There is no magic wand.”

articles.content: Anthropic announced new workplace features on Tuesday, including Claude Meetings, which brings Claude into video calls to begin working on tasks while participants are still talking. The company also unveiled Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets. The launch of Anthropic’s new productivity-focused features comes just a few weeks after OpenAI unveiled a series of workplace tools that allow users to collaborate with ChatGPT to do things like visualize company information and create presentations, as both companies compete to turn their products into office suites of sorts to take on Microsoft and Google. Meta is also joining the competition with its Muse AI agent, which can build mini-apps on the fly to help users complete specific tasks. With Claude Meetings, teams can add Claude to a video call as a visible participant. Claude then follows the conversation and gets to work on tasks in real time. As participants talk, it can draft the plan being discussed, map out a timeline on a whiteboard, answer questions in the meeting chat, and access connected work apps to retrieve information, such as last year’s figures. After the call, the meeting notes, action items, and other materials Claude created are available in claude.ai. The work that comes out of a meeting usually starts after everyone hangs up, but with this new feature, teams can turn discussions into actions in real time, Anthropic says. Claude identifies itself as a meeting participant and posts a notice in the meeting chat. It won’t join calls with external guests unless authorized by an admin, and will automatically leave if an external guest joins. Claude Meetings is launching in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. At launch, it works with Google Meet, with support for additional plans expected to follow. As for Claude Whiteboards, Anthropic describes the feature as a collaborative board where teams can talk through a plan and have Claude turn it into an organized visual workspace with timelines and deadlines. The company notes that many people already brainstorm with Claude, but that in order to share their results with others, they would have to copy-paste them somewhere else. Now, a team can work directly with Claude on the same board in real time. When the brainstorm is done, Claude can turn the board into a doc or a slide deck. Additionally, Whiteboards also work inside Claude Meetings, so the board builds while people talk, Anthropic says. Claude Whiteboards is available in beta on paid plans, on web, desktop, and mobile. The company also launched Claude Sheets, which lets teams create and collaboratively edit spreadsheets with Claude. A team can ask it to build a campaign tracker or hiring budget, and Claude will then generate a working spreadsheet. Anthropic says Claude handles the initial setup of trackers and budgets, while allowing teams to continue refining and updating the same spreadsheet. Each spreadsheet can include multiple tabs, formulas, formatting, and dropdown menus. Claude also makes edits directly in cells alongside the team, and outlines each change so users can see what it did. Claude Sheets is available in beta on paid plans, on web, desktop and mobile. Anthropic also announced that Claude Data, formerly known as Claude Dashboards, is now generally available. The feature connects Claude to systems that companies use to keep their numbers, like a data warehouse or CRM. Users can ask questions, and Claude responds with dashboards, written data stories, or narrated videos. Additionally, the company announced interactive connectors that open the full version of apps like Adobe, Atlassian, and HubSpot inside Claude. Anthropic notes that teams can now open these apps directly alongside their Claude conversations and ask the assistant to work within them, essentially bringing existing workflows into the same workspace. articles.content: Since Valve announced its Steam Deck Verified program in 2021, players have found that a game's "Verified" status doesn't always match how well it actually runs on the handheld. Now, new Steam Deck frame rate data being shared by Valve itself can help players dig deeper into the performance they can expect from many Steam Deck games. Valve has been collecting anonymized frame rate data from Steam players who opt in since February. Yesterday evening, the company announced it has started sharing that data on many Steam Store pages as averages and histograms for both the Steam Deck and Steam Deck OLED. Valve acknowledges that players enabling VSync or frame rate limits can bias the collected data somewhat and that the measurements don't account for custom in-game settings that Steam Deck users may tinker with to get a game running. articles.content: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is quietly working towards a new goal: to become a progressive kingmaker in the burgeoning battle for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination. The socialist mayor of the nation's most populous city, who can't run for president himself because he's not a natural-born U.S. citizen, has been meeting behind closed doors with labor leaders to highlight the need for a union-aligned or left-wing candidate to seek the presidency. The mayor's moves come as he's reportedly said he's uncertain whether progressive champion Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, his close political ally, will run for the White House. According to Axios, which was first to report the news, Mamdani is concerned that if Ocasio-Cortez stays out of the 2028 race, it could leave progressives without a standard-bearer to face off against a more centrist presidential frontrunner in the primary battle. WILL TRUMP SIT OUT MAKING A 2028 ENDORSEMENT IN THE RACE TO SUCCEED HIM? Mamdani, who is seen as a major powerbroker for the left wing of the Democratic Party after his historic 2025 mayoral election victory, argues that the progressive movement can't waste its momentum coming out of last week's trouncing of Republicans in the midterm elections, as Democrats won a massive House majority and control of the Senate. A source familiar with Mamdani's 2028 conversations told Axios the mayor "wants the progressive ecosystem to mobilize quickly, strategically and efficiently if a moderate candidate is clearly on the rise," Meanwhile, Ocasio-Cortez is publicly pumping the brakes on speculation she'll launch a presidential campaign or bid for the Senate in New York, even as a newly formed group of activists is urging her run for the White House. VANCE, CRUZ, DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS 2028 BATTLE BEGINS "I think the thing that's important here is the last thing that people want to hear from me or any other politician here is about the next election. And what they actually want to hear from us is about what we are going to do with the electoral results they just gave us on Tuesday," Ocasio-Cortez told reporters Monday night, pointing to the midterms. The comments from Ocasio-Cortez, who was re-elected last week to a fifth term representing parts of New York City, came hours after the formal launch of Ready for AOC, a political group working to encourage her to run for president by showing her she has legions of supporters ready to mobilize on her behalf. "A people-powered movement asking Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for President in 2028. No campaign. No money. Just names," is how the group described itself on social media. But Ocasio-Cortez said voters are more concerned about congressional Democrats' immediate legislative agenda rather than speculating about the next election. "I think people are less concerned about the horse race, and they want to know: What are the investigations we're going to be starting? What is the legislation that we're going to be starting?" she said. Veteran Democratic strategist David Plouffe, campaign manager for former President Barack Obama's landmark 2008 White House victory and a senior advisor on then-Vice President Kamala Harris' 2024 bid, said last week, "If AOC runs, she's going to start, 20-25%, probably. The question is, can she add to that? If she doesn't run, then that is wide open. That's where I think someone like Abdul may say, 'Even though I just won, should I look at it?'" SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Plouffe, who was speaking at a forum hosted by Harvard University's Institute of Politics, was referring to Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who made history last week as the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. "That's the thing about this race. It's so wide open that there may be some people run who surprise us. I also think there'll be some people who don't run who'll surprise us," Plouffe added. Ocasio-Cortez said in September that she's weighing what to do next, whether it be a White House run or a bid for the seat currently held by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a fellow Democrat and New Yorker. "I know there is a lot of speculation about what I will decide to do in 2028. I get asked about it nearly every interview and event," Ocasio-Cortez wrote in a fundraising email to supporters. The now-37-year-old lawmaker with a massive social media footprint said in a New York Times interview two months ago that her decision, which could happen sometime after the midterm elections, would come down to answering the question, "Where can I do the most good?" Schumer, who turns 76 later this month, has left his 2028 plans open and has not announced whether he’ll run for sixth six-year term in the Senate. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Ocasio-Cortez isn't the only leading figure on the left who is mulling a presidential run. So is Rep. Ro Khanna of California, a top House progressive. Allies of the soon-to-be six-term congressman last week launched a draft committee called "Run Ro" to build support and raise funds for a potential 2028 presidential campaign.

Individuals representing the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics ballot committee, Clean […]
articles.content: Michiganders for Money Out of Politics submitted its signatures in Lansing to make the November 2026 ballot. May 27, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Three groups that supported and organized the “Michiganders for Money Out of Politics” ballot measure that passed on Nov. 3, as well as a recently elected state representative, have filed a motion to intervene in two First Amendment lawsuits filed against the measure. Individuals representing the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics ballot committee, Clean Water Action and Voters Not Politicians, as well as state Rep.-elect Joanna Whaley, argued in their brief that the current defendants — Attorney General Dana Nessel, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and, in the suit from the utilities, Director of Elections Jonathan Brater — “represent the public at large” and as such, have different considerations in defending the lawsuit. “These include Defendants’ obligations to take account of enforcement priorities and resource limits and their interest in preserving enforcement discretion,” the brief argues. “These interests may lead Defendants to concede the invalidity of certain applications of Proposal 2 or agree to narrowing constructions to it, or even to enter into a settlement of the case. Proposed Intervenors, by contrast, have a direct stake in every provision of Proposal 2.” Because of this, the groups argue that they should be included as defendants in the lawsuit in order to defend the interests of those who drafted and advocated for the proposal. All three organizations were involved in the creation of the ballot measure and collection of signatures on its petition, and each advocated for its passage. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE For Whaley, the motion states that during her 2026 campaign, she “faced advertisements, supported by outside spending, that did not use the ‘magic words’ of ‘vote for’ or ‘vote against’ and thus would not trigger disclosures under the law prior to Proposal 2 but that would trigger disclosures under Proposal 2. She intends to run for re-election and expects to confront similar outside spending in her reelection campaign.” In support of their motion, the groups also argue that in the past, courts “have repeatedly granted permissive intervention to the sponsors of ballot initiatives in cases challenging the adoption or implementation of those initiatives.” Both lawsuits — one brought by the right-leaning policy think tank Mackinac Center and the other brought by utility companies — were filed in the days after the election. The proposal to ban campaign spending from regulated electric and gas utilities and from major government contractors passed with over 80% support. In a press release from the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics campaign, longtime federal litigator Samuel Bagenstos says that the group is “fully confident in the legality of Proposal 2 and look forward to seeing this out in court.” Bagenstos, who is representing the proposed intervenor-defendants along with Stephanie Command and Tracey Wigglesworth of The Political Law Group, added, “The language of Proposal 2 was carefully crafted with constitutionality in mind, and we are well prepared for this expected legal challenge. We intend to vigorously defend the will of Michiganders who overwhelmingly approved this measure just one week ago.”

articles.title: High oil prices have led to a dip in global carbon emissions
articles.description: Bucking recent trends, fossil fuel emissions look to be down 0.4 percent.
articles.content: Evaluating the annual global temperatures each year requires context. There is a fair amount of natural variability from one year to the next, so it’s important to focus on the trend over time. Famously, global warming did not end in 1998, as some claimed a couple of decades ago—we just had a run of La-Niña-dominated years after a very strong El Niño. Annual greenhouse gas emissions are much less variable, having increased fairly steadily, but many complicating factors can still muddy the picture. Sometimes those factors conspire to throw a year off the trend. It looks like 2026 will be one of those years. A new analysis led by Corinne Le Quéré at the University of East Anglia estimates that fossil fuel emissions have fallen about 0.4 percent from last year. This probably isn’t a peak that symbolizes heartening progress on climate change, though; the researchers think it’s a short-term dip driven by the war in Iran and its effect on oil prices.Read full article Comments
