articles.title: As ‘child predator hunters’ go viral, states grapple with the risks of civilian stings
articles.description: Across the country, dozens of civilian groups, or vigilantes, are posing as children online, arranging meetings with adults they suspect of seeking sex with minors and livestreaming the confrontations to thousands of viewers. The groups say they are helping protect children and bring suspected predators to justice. But some law enforcement officials and legal experts […]
articles.content: Harford County, Md., Sheriff Jeff Gahler speaks with Chris Hansen, the host of “Takedown with Chris Hansen” on the TruBlu streaming network. The sheriff’s office conducted several operations featured on the show to highlight how local investigators identify and apprehend suspected child predators. (Photo courtesy of Harford County Sheriff’s Office)Across the country, dozens of civilian groups, or vigilantes, are posing as children online, arranging meetings with adults they suspect of seeking sex with minors and livestreaming the confrontations to thousands of viewers. The groups say they are helping protect children and bring suspected predators to justice. But some law enforcement officials and legal experts warn that their tactics can jeopardize criminal investigations, complicate prosecutions and put public safety at risk. Public accusations can also have lasting consequences for people who are never charged with a crime, while some groups encourage their followers to pressure police to make arrests. There is no definitive count of civilian predator-hunting groups, but dozens of groups operate across different parts of the country, including major cities. Stateline identified nearly 50 individuals or groups nationwide that have posted online content exposing suspected child predators. For state lawmakers and law enforcement officials, the growing presence of these groups adds another layer of complexity to efforts to combat online child sexual exploitation while protecting children and preserving the integrity of criminal investigations. “What is beyond dispute is we have a massive problem of child exploitation in this country that takes various forms,” said Mary Graw Leary, a law professor at the Catholic University of America whose work focuses on the exploitation of women and children. Graw Leary is a former state and federal prosecutor. “We cannot criminalize our way out of it only because there’s just too much of it.” Catching and prosecuting people who sexually exploit children is important, experts say, but it addresses only part of the problem. Preventing abuse also requires teaching adults and children to recognize warning signs, creating environments where children feel safe speaking up and are heard, and holding institutions and online platforms accountable. “The criminal justice response, I think, is appropriate, warranted, and important, but it’s not the only thing that we should be doing as a society or as communities,” said Stacy Vaughan, the vice president of growth and prevention at Childhelp, a nonprofit dedicated to preventing and responding to child abuse. When a viral video isn’t enough The scale of online child sexual exploitation is immense. The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children received 21.3 million reports through its CyberTipline in 2025, including about 1.4 million reports of online enticement of children for sexual acts — a 158% increase from 2024 –– and more than 19.5 million reports involving child sexual abuse material. Popularized by NBC’s Dateline series “To Catch a Predator,” which aired in the early 2000s, civilian predator-hunting groups use adult decoys posing as children or teenagers online to contact people they suspect of seeking sex with minors, then confront them on camera. The accusations can make for compelling viral content. People accused of targeting children often have little public sympathy, and videos promising to expose and humiliate them can attract viewers with little interest in what happens after the camera shuts off. Quotation The best way for these groups to be helpful would be for them to involve law enforcement when they get the first nibble on their line. – Matt Irvine, a retired detective who investigated sex crimes in California and Oregon Some vigilante groups involve law enforcement only after a sting is complete, or if a confrontation turns violent. That can leave responding officers with an incomplete picture of what happened, how the encounter unfolded and whether the evidence supports criminal charges. Digital evidence — the online conversations and promises — must be authenticated and preserved to establish its origin, integrity and handling. Recordings can also raise legal questions, experts say, including whether groups violated state wiretapping laws when capturing private conversations. “The best way for these groups to be helpful would be for them to involve law enforcement when they get the first nibble on their line,” said Matt Irvine, a retired detective with 29 years of law enforcement experience who investigated sex crimes and cold-case sexual assaults in California and Oregon. When police are involved from the start, he said, detectives can conduct a more thorough investigation, check a suspect’s criminal history and obtain search warrants. The financial arrangements behind the videos can raise additional concerns if group members are called as witnesses in criminal cases. Some groups can earn advertising revenue from videos posted online, while others offer paid memberships through platforms such as YouTube, Rumble, Kick and Locals, where subscribers can get earlier or exclusive access than nonmembers to videos, updates, unedited footage and chat logs. Those financial incentives could become relevant in court, particularly if prosecutors or defense attorneys question whether a witness had a financial interest in producing a confrontation or attracting viewers. “If they are selling the confrontation videos and profiting from that, that would be an ethical issue in a criminal case,” said Kelly Callihan, the executive director of the Pennsylvania District Attorneys Association. “If we’re going to call them as a witness, that would have to be something that we would disclose to the defense.” Some predator-catching groups also criticize police or prosecutors when a person is not arrested or charged, encouraging viewers to contact and complain to officials about their decisions. “These predator groups now, I feel like, are escalating from shaming the alleged perpetrators of these acts to crossing a line where they’re shaming district attorneys who aren’t bringing these charges, even though they have valid reasons not to do so,” Callihan said. Public confrontations Videos of civilian predator-catching operations sometimes show violent confrontations. In one viral video from 2024, members of Dads Against Predators surround a man at an H-E-B grocery store in Austin, Texas, and strike him in the back of the head with a pumpkin. The man, James Schellhase, filed a federal racketeering lawsuit against the Ohio-based group in September, alleging that its members assaulted him, tried to extort him and cost him his job as a chief executive. Schellhase had been communicating online with people who later claimed to be minors, according to the lawsuit. He said he believed the interaction was a prank or scam and wanted to confront them. The group accused him of trying to meet a child for sex. Schellhase alleges that Dads Against Predators demanded $400,000 to keep the confrontation video from being released and that the footage was sent to his employer, according to the lawsuit. He says the encounter damaged his career. One of the group’s co-founders, Joshua Alvin Mundy, has denied wrongdoing. Dads Against Predators has been linked to multiple suicides involving people the group filmed. The group has also faced scrutiny from law enforcement in California, Florida, North Carolina and Texas, where members have been arrested or authorities have urged them to stop their activities. In 2020, the Sandusky County Sheriff’s Office in Ohio warned the group that it could face prosecution if it continued its “vigilante efforts.” But the concerns extend beyond physical safety. Public accusations may also target people who have committed no crime and jeopardize investigations by alerting suspects before police can gather evidence, identify additional victims or pursue other leads. In April of this year, livestreamer Vitaly Zdorovetskiy and his crew falsely accused a 25-year-old man of trying to meet a 16-year-old girl for sex during a confrontation at a Southern California park, prompting online harassment of the man and his family. Police detained the man, but released him after questioning, and Zdorovetskiy later apologized for the mistaken accusation, but clips of the confrontation continued circulating online. Public confrontations can also expose civilian predator hunters themselves to potential criminal charges, especially if encounters turn violent or involve threats. For some groups, that tension has changed how they operate. Brian Knepp founded 814 Pred Hunters in Pennsylvania in 2022 after learning that a man he had considered a friend had raped a child. The group initially focused on publicly confronting suspected predators and exposing them online, but frustration over local prosecutors’ inability to bring charges prompted Knepp to change course and seek closer cooperation with police and prosecutors. “We wanted these guys to be held accountable, and just us exposing them, in my mind, wasn’t acceptable anymore,” Knepp said in an interview. Josh Moody, chief operating officer of Alabama-based Covenant Rescue Group, a nonprofit that trains police, said effective undercover operations require preparation and coordination. The group’s training covers evidence handling, communication, intelligence gathering and surveillance, as well as avoiding conduct that could undermine a prosecution, including actions that could support an entrapment defense. The group generally does not post any content online. “If we come in and do a one-off operation and arrest a few guys on the operation –– that’s great, but really, we want (law enforcement) to be able to continue the work,” Moody said. Some law enforcement agencies have adopted a different approach to publicizing undercover operations, partnering with television programs while maintaining control over investigations and evidence. Sheriffs Chris Swanson of Genesee County, Michigan, and Jeff Gahler of Harford County, Maryland, whose investigations have been featured on the TruBlu series “Takedown with Chris Hansen,” described how their agencies conduct these operations. Swanson said G.H.O.S.T., the office’s specialized sex crimes unit, conducts investigations that can span months, involving background checks, surveillance, recorded online conversations and interviews. Investigators do not pursue people who chat online but never show up at a planned meeting location. Since 2018, which is when the unit was founded, more than 270 people have been prosecuted in connection with these investigations, Swanson said. He said the Chris Hansen segments take place in a controlled environment, and footage is not used in investigations. His office provides exculpatory video to both prosecutors and defense attorneys. He sees media partnerships such as the Chris Hansen show as a way to raise awareness and encourage victims to seek help. By contrast, he warned that civilian groups seeking viral content without coordinating with law enforcement can jeopardize investigations. “We’re going to keep doing it, and we’re going to do it the right way,” Swanson said. Gahler said his office has arrested at least 21 people in three separate operations in partnership with the show, adding that the public attention they generate serves as a strong deterrent. “That’s part of why we do this job — to deter crime and prevent crime,” Gahler said. Beyond the confrontation Others disagree. Former detective Matt Irvine said public exposure can work against another important goal of an investigation: getting suspects to talk. In his experience investigating sex crimes and cold-case sexual assaults, interviews are more effective when investigators build rapport in a calm, controlled setting. Public confrontations designed to humiliate suspects can undermine those efforts, he said, making it harde

articles.title: Disaster aid becomes political lottery: Libraries, schools and places of worship step into breach
articles.description: Daniel P. Aldrich, Northeastern University Four tornadoes tore across southwest Michigan in early March 2026, killing four people. They were the state’s deadliest natural hazards in decades. Gov. Gretchen Whitmer asked the Federal Emergency Management Agency for assistance to cover uninsured and underinsured losses. FEMA said no. She appealed. FEMA said no again. I study […]
articles.content: Volunteers assess tornado damage in Union City, Mich., on March 7, 2026. Nam Y. Huh/AP PhotoDaniel P. Aldrich, Northeastern University Four tornadoes tore across southwest Michigan in early March 2026, killing four people. They were the state’s deadliest natural hazards in decades. Gov. Gretchen Whitmer asked the Federal Emergency Management Agency for assistance to cover uninsured and underinsured losses. FEMA said no. She appealed. FEMA said no again. I study how communities prepare for and recover from disasters. As Dean’s Professor of Resilience at Northeastern University, I have written six books on the topic, including the forthcoming “Beyond Common Ground.” The fact that Michigan was repeatedly denied aid reflects a broader shift, one that is putting more weight on the ties between neighbors and the places where they meet. Federal help is less predictable The Trump administration denied 26% of major disaster declarations in 2025, more than double the rate of the year before and well above the 15% denial average of the past two decades. Denials have not fallen evenly. One study looked at some 2,500 disaster declarations since FEMA’s creation in 1979 in states where the governor and U.S. senators were all Republican or all Democrat. In his second term, Trump approved nearly 90% of requests from all-Republican states while approving only 23% of those from all-Democratic states. Colorado, an all-Democratic state, had both of its 2025 appeals for disaster rejected. They were Colorado’s first denials since the 1980s. Florida, an all-Republican state, fared differently. In June, Trump announced US$416 million for the state’s disasters without specifying which one, adding that much of it would go to the Panhandle, one of his “favorite places.” There, a January 2025 snowstorm was linked to 13 deaths and caused approximately $200 million in damages. Nationally, an analysis of FEMA data by Andrew Rumbach, a senior fellow at the Urban Institute, found that about 84% of requests from states Trump won in 2024 were approved during his second term, compared with about 42% from states he lost. While the White House has denied that politics plays a role in who receives aid after shocks, local communities are now shouldering more of the cost of preparing for, responding to and recovering from disasters than they did before 2025. FEMA owes local governments almost $10 billion in reimbursements for recovery work that cities and towns have already paid for. When a declaration is denied, towns can be left covering costs as high as 15% of their annual budget. Philanthropies and aid groups such as Team Rubicon are expanding their roles to fill the gaps. Nonprofits and community organizations cannot replace federal funding, but they can build cooperation, trust and collective action, which can better prepare neighborhoods and accelerate recovery. What connected places do In Union City, Michigan, help arrived within hours of the EF3 tornado that killed three people in March 2026. It came not from Washington but from neighbors. School administrators turned the local high school into a shelter the night of the storm, volunteers arrived with food and supplies, and the local United Way opened a relief fund. That is typical: Local residents are almost always the first responders after disasters strike. What was different is that federal help never followed. Donations poured into the local high school, and the superintendent said staff worked out how to get supplies to the people who needed them. A local church, damaged in the storm, started a disaster fund to help residents pay their insurance deductibles. Research on U.S. disasters shows how places such as schools, faith-based organizations and libraries can keep communities knit together. After Hurricane Katrina in August 2005, floodwaters as high as 12 feet (3.6 meters) covered the low-income neighborhood around the Mary Queen of Vietnam Church in east New Orleans. Yet by summer 2007, about 90% of its residents had returned to their homes. For the city as a whole, the figure hit only 45%. The difference was likely the leadership of the Rev. Vien Nguyen, who coordinated supplies, organized volunteers and kept scattered residents in touch even as they evacuated to other states. In 2005, Bishop Dominic Loung returned home from Houston, Texas, to Mary Queen of Vietnam Church in New Orleans to survey damage from Hurricane Katrina. Rick Loomis/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images My lab’s research during the COVID-19 pandemic found a similar pattern. We compared U.S. counties that were alike in many ways but differed in their social ties. After accounting for politics, governance, healthcare quality and demographics, our study found that two kinds of ties reduced the pandemic’s toll: bonding ties and linking ties. Bonding ties connect neighbors and family. Linking ties connect residents to officials. Those ties are often built through spaces designed for connection, such as libraries and faith-based organizations like Nguyen’s church in New Orleans. Libraries continue to safeguard our most vulnerable. In 2025, 44.7% of U.S. public libraries served as cooling or warming centers during extreme temperatures, up 8.2% from 2022. Many could do more. In a national survey, 84% of library directors agreed that libraries have a critical role in disaster response. Yet only 36% knew that federal law allows libraries to seek FEMA relocation funding to move to safer ground, and just 51% had an emergency preparedness plan. A low-cost layer of protection In my new book, I show that more than 90% of federal disaster funds went to roads, utilities and other standard infrastructure in the early 21st century, and less than 10% to libraries, parks, schools, places of worship and community centers, where neighbors check on one another and organize recovery. Federal aid may go to rebuild some of these spaces, but it rarely pays to keep them open and running when communities need them most. In another study, I found that Japanese communities with higher density of social infrastructure had half the number of deaths from a catastrophic tsunami in March 2011 compared to similar communities with fewer gathering spaces. In my assessment, as federal aid becomes less predictable, these kinds of places people frequent often will have to carry us into the future. The communities that recover best from the next disaster may be the ones that kept their libraries open, their civic halls full of volunteers and their parks full of residents. Daniel P. Aldrich, Professor of Political Science, Public Policy and Urban Affairs, Northeastern University. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. articles.title: Apple TV makes sign language interpretation a built-in accessibility feature
articles.description: Apple TV's new accessibility feature lets viewers turn on sign language interpretation within supported titles.
articles.content: Apple TV is making its content more accessible to Deaf audiences with the launch of a new Sign Language Interpretation feature, the company announced on Tuesday. The feature will initially be available across a limited set of titles, starting this Friday with the release of “Being Heumann,” a biopic about disability rights activist Judy Heumann. American Sign Language (ASL) and British Sign Language (BSL) will also be made available for Apple’s hit movie “F1.” Later this year, other titles will follow, including “Way of the Warrior Kid” and “Greyhound.” What makes Apple’s offering different from other platforms is that the sign language version of the film is not a separate product — that is, it’s not a separate film designed just for Deaf viewers. Instead, Apple’s support for sign language is just a setting you enable that’s integrated with the main title, similar to how you could turn on or off closed captions. When a title with the sign language option is playing, an interpreter appears in the bottom right of the screen, translating the spoken words into signs. Apple says it has partnered with a group of DASLs (Directors of Artistic Sign Language) to ensure that the interpreter for each film fits the tone of the film. Notably, the company is not using any AI-generated interpreters, as Apple says that’s not what the Deaf community has said it needs. The feature is shipping in the latest release of iOS 27.2, and can be turned on through a new sign language option in Settings. After being enabled, a new button will appear in the supported Apple Original titles on Apple TV indicating that sign language is available. These titles are labeled with a sign language icon that appears on the title page alongside other features like closed captions or audio descriptions. There’s also a new section under languages that will list the specific sign languages that are available with the given title. To make the titles more discoverable, Apple TV will highlight which titles include the sign language option in a “Movies & Shows with American Sign Language” editorial collection. Meanwhile, users can easily surface supported titles via search by typing in keywords like “with ASL,” for example. The new feature builds on Apple’s other investments in accessibility features, which it builds itself. “At Apple, we believe everyone should be able to enjoy great stories and entertainment,” said Sarah Herrlinger, Apple’s senior director of Global Accessibility Policy and Initiatives, in a statement about the launch. “Bringing sign language interpretation to Apple TV is an exciting step forward in making the viewing experience more accessible and inclusive for Deaf audiences. Accessibility is a core value at Apple, and we’re proud to continue creating experiences that allow more people to enjoy the content they love,” she added. articles.title: Parents of Michigan students with disabilities demand special education reforms
articles.description: More than 75 people attended a meeting Monday night focused on what the state can do to improve special education. Many shared personal stories of their students.
articles.content: More than 75 people attend a state meeting about special education Parents raised concerns about students receiving specialized services, communication with local schools and student discipline Attendees told Bridge they hope state officials take their concerns seriously and make changes SAGINAW — Dozens of Michigan parents and advocates gathered Monday to demand that local schools and state officials provide more support for students with disabilities. This story also appeared in Bridge Michigan More than 75 people packed a State Board of Education Special Education Committee meeting in Saginaw. It was the committee’s first public meeting outside of Lansing since the state board formed the bipartisan group in June and charged it with finding ways to improve services for students with disabilities. “We acknowledge that we are in a tough place,” State Board of Education president Pamela Pugh, a Democrat from Saginaw, told the audience. “We acknowledge that we do not have all the answers. We acknowledge that this process is something that we set out to do, not even knowing which direction to go in, but knowing that we needed to continue to hear from parents.” Parents shared stories of students with disabilities not receiving enough specialized services to learn in their classrooms and instances where parents had to battle their local schools. Terricina Jackson, an advocate in Saginaw and parent of a 9-year-old son with autism, said she hopes “the state holds the administrators and the district responsible for the violation of children’s rights, the implementation of IEPs (individualized education programs), the data that is not being provided to families.” Related: Michigan wants to scrap rarely used special ed rule. Child advocates fear harm Report: Michigan must overhaul ‘inequitable’ way it funds special education A renewed push to ban seclusion, reduce restraint in Michigan schools Michigan fight over special ed services lingers, years after COVID shutdown “I want the board to hold these schools accountable, the ISD accountable for the lack that we are all experiencing. I’m not sure that’s going to happen. “ Terricina Jackson, an advocate and parent of a 9-year-old with autism, told Bridge she hopes state officials hold local districts accountable for their actions. (Isabel Lohman/ Bridge Michigan) Jackson said Monday’s meeting involved “a bunch of photo opps. I think that they allowed us to express our concern because they know that families need to be heard, but actually implementing, I’ve not seen anybody do that in five years.” Attendees told Bridge they want schools to provide support for students and for the state to hold schools accountable for their actions. Sarah Earle, a parent of a 14-year-old, told Bridge she hopes her family’s and others’ concerns are heard and “that change is made” across the state. “These kids deserve the very best just like everybody else.” Attendees shared experiences in small groups with their discussions recorded on AI tools. The state plans to compile responses from multiple meetings. In one small group, participants discussed students needing one-on-one paraprofessionals, changes to state teacher credentials, and concerns that students are losing out on key help that would allow them to learn. “Parents should not have to reach a breaking point to get their children help,” said Jennifer Gruesbeck of Saginaw township during the public comment portion of the meeting. “We should not have to become experts in special education, constantly advocate, document every incident, attend endless meetings, put our jobs in jeopardy, and fight for basic services just to ensure our children have access to an education.” Small groups discuss their concerns during a breakout session at the Michigan Department of Education’s Special Education Committee meeting in Saginaw on Monday, Nov. 9. (Courtesy of the Michigan Department of Education) Some traveled far to share their experience. Carrie Dickerson, a parent and advocate, said she travelled two hours to attend the meeting. “While efforts to travel the state are appreciated, many families cannot make a trip like this.” Dickerson said. “Parents of children with disabilities often face significant barriers, including work schedules, caregiving responsibilities, transportation challenges, and disability-related needs of their own or their children.” The committee plans to hold meetings in Oakland, Grand Traverse and Marquette counties in the future, according to a news release. The dates for these meetings have not yet been publicly released. Pugh said the committee also plans to hold virtual sessions. There were 226,800 Michigan students receiving special education last school year in Michigan public, private or homeschool settings. They’re part of a system some say is filled with problems. Schools continue to face high special education teacher shortages, and as of last year, Michigan had one of the nation’s highest rates of special education drop outs. Christopher Earle and Sarah Earle attended the State Board of Education Special Education Committee Monday, Nov. 9 with hopes state officials will change education for their 14-year-old son and other students with disabilities. (Isabel Lohman/Bridge Michigan) Michigan reimburses local districts for a percentage of the cost of providing special ed services and transportation. That’s in addition to a per-pupil foundation allowance from the state’s School Aid Fund. Last year, advocates called for the state to move toward a weighted funding model that provides more state money for students with the highest needs., arguing the current system is inequitable. Meanwhile, parents and advocates have raised concerns about the state’s complaint process which allows a parent to file a free complaint against their local district. A 2025 Bridge examination of state records found that since 2018, state investigations stemming from parent complaints had jumped 21%, while the overall population of special education students increased just 3.6%. Advocates previously told Bridge the system was stacked against parents — making them fight for services that are supposed to be guaranteed by law. Kourtney Sabourin, a parent of an 11-year-old with autism, told Bridge she has filed four state complaints and “every time I’ve been dissatisfied.” She said districts know they “are going to get a slap on the hand” by the state if they violate rules, but “they’re not afraid of anything and students continue to suffer.” The meeting on Monday comes as the Michigan Department of Education analyzes public comment over a set of changes it’s proposing to special education rules. One contentious idea is to scrap the so-called “stay put” provision. Currently, when a parent or guardian files a special education complaint with the state, the department can require that the student remain in their current classroom or specialized program while it investigates. But MDE says the stay-put provision applies to legal proceedings rather than departmental investigations and that it has only been invoked once in the 47-year history of the state complaint process. It says the change aligns with federal disability law. The Autism Alliance of Michigan and other student advocacy groups are opposed to the proposal State Superintendent Glenn Maleyko, who attended Monday’s meeting, said that since he started a listening tour in February, special education is the top concern. “We know it’s very important,” Maleyko said. “It’s probably one of the more challenging areas of education, but we really need to work together.” This article first appeared on Bridge Michigan and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.

articles.title: Defense Secretary Hegseth calls impeachment push a ‘farce’ as US House heads toward vote
articles.description: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth struck a defiant tone Tuesday as he faces potential impeachment by the U.S. House of Representatives this week, casting the effort as an attack on American service members. Hegseth during a rare news conference at the Pentagon called the impeachment effort a “farce” and flatly rejected the notion that he had […]
articles.content: U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth listens to question during a news conference at the Pentagon on March 2, 2026 in Arlington, Virginia. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth struck a defiant tone Tuesday as he faces potential impeachment by the U.S. House of Representatives this week, casting the effort as an attack on American service members. Hegseth during a rare news conference at the Pentagon called the impeachment effort a “farce” and flatly rejected the notion that he had committed impeachable offenses as the top civilian leader of the military. He likened himself to President Donald Trump, who was twice impeached during his first term. “Let’s be clear about what this resolution actually does. It tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations,” Hegseth said. The House, led by Republicans during the lame-duck session following the Nov. 3 election, is set to vote on impeaching Hegseth as soon as Wednesday, with a procedural vote expected later Tuesday. Massie impeachment articles Rep. Thomas Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, introduced articles of impeachment Monday alleging the defense secretary waged unlawful war against Iran, ordered extrajudicial killings and ignored laws intended to minimize civilian casualties, among other charges. Impeachment would represent an extraordinary rebuke of one of the most divisive members of Trump’s Cabinet. Democrats, as well as some Republicans, are expected to support the effort, raising the possibility the articles will pass and trigger a trial in the Senate, though the outcome is unclear there. Hegseth, a 46-year-old former Fox News personality who narrowly won Senate confirmation last year, has sought to project a swashbuckling, masculine image as the military’s top civilian leader. He has rebranded the Department of Defense as the “Department of War,” purged numerous high-ranking officers and tried to kick critical media outlets out of the Pentagon. On Tuesday, Hegseth called Massie a “disgruntled and defeated congressman” who is attempting a “political spectacle” driven by ego and resentment. Massie, who has often clashed with Trump, lost his primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger. “It’s a farce and it’s a stunt and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said. Drug boats Massie told reporters on Monday that Hegseth’s conduct of the military has endangered Americans. As an example, he pointed to a second strike conducted on survivors of a suspected drug boat in the Caribbean that had already been hit, suggesting it will encourage enemies of the U.S. to act similarly in the future. Hegseth has denied ordering the strike, but said he supported it. Massie dismissed Hegseth’s attacks on him, adding that he was “being polite” by using the impeachment process, which would only remove Hegseth from office but not subject him to criminal charges. “Well, he’s right about one thing, I’m a defeated congressman. I’m not disgruntled,” Massie said. The House can impeach Hegseth with a simple majority vote, though GOP leaders may first attempt to derail the measure with procedural votes, such as sending the articles to a committee. But convicting Hegseth and removing him as defense secretary will take a two-thirds vote in the Senate — 67 senators — a high bar to clear. The Senate is currently composed of 53 Republicans and 47 Democrats, including two independent senators who caucus with Democrats. Beginning in January, Democrats will control the chamber with at least 54 seats. Trump praise Trump has so far stood by Hegseth. He praised the defense secretary in multiple public remarks over the past two weeks, saying he’s “done a fantastic job” in reducing the number of “woke” four-star generals, and for conducting the “war with Venezuela,” which he said “was over in 48 minutes.” “Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached. Congress, stand up for Pete!!!” Trump wrote in a social media post on Monday. Impeachment would mark a significant escalation in Congress’ push to restrain Trump’s war in Iran — and its efforts to assert authority over presidential warmaking. The U.S. Constitution grants Congress the power to declare war, something lawmakers haven’t done since World War II. The U.S. military, in conjunction with Israeli forces, attacked Iran in late February. The American campaign, overseen by Hegseth, killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and numerous other Iranian officials. Iran retaliated by firing missiles at U.S. bases across the Middle East and moving to cut off traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, a critical shipping point for oil. The lack of safe, regular access to the strait has sent energy prices rising in the U.S. and around the world. War Powers Resolution The articles of impeachment include three articles alleging Hegseth directed military operations against Iran in violation of the War Powers Resolution, legislation Congress approved in 1973 over the veto of President Richard Nixon. The War Powers Resolution sets limits on when presidents can engage in military conflict without authorization by Congress. The legality of the War Powers Resolution has long been disputed, with the executive branch asserting it improperly interferes with the president’s conduct of foreign policy. Secretary of State Marco Rubio as recently as May called the War Powers Resolution unconstitutional. Impeachment would signal that executive branch officials could face consequences if they don’t abide by the War Powers Resolution. “Pete Hegseth is obligated to follow the laws on the books, not the laws that he wants to follow,” Massie said Monday. Hegseth disputed the allegations, saying he had overseen lawful military operations first ordered by Trump. He said initiating the impeachment effort ahead of Veterans Day on Wednesday sends a message to service members that “their service was a crime.” “We destroyed terror regimes’ capabilities. We sank the boats carrying poison into our communities. We put a narco dictator in handcuffs,” Hegseth said. “These are not high crimes. This is the job, and it’s a job well done.” Next Congress Massie, who has said he would drop his impeachment effort if Hegseth resigns, suggested that the defense secretary will face more intense scrutiny in the next Congress if he survives the current impeachment effort. Democrats, Massie said, will hold hearings on Hegseth’s conduct that could prompt more Republican senators to vote to convict him. Democrats will have a strong majority in the House beginning in January and will almost certainly have enough votes to impeach Hegseth if Massie’s effort comes up short. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat expected to become speaker in January, told reporters Monday that he is a “hard yes” on Massie’s articles of impeachment. “He’s the architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran,” Jeffries said of Hegseth. On Monday, Trump told reporters at the White House that Hegseth had won two wars, referring to the conflicts in Iran and Venezuela, where U.S. special forces seized President Nicolás Maduro in a nighttime raid. Maduro is now awaiting trial in the United States on federal narco-terrorism charges. Eighteen U.S. service members have died since the start of the war in Iran on Feb. 28, with the most recent deaths in July, according to the Defense Casualty Analysis System. No service members died in Venezuela. Trump questioned why leaders who oversaw past wars with far higher casualty counts weren’t impeached. “We lost 18 — 18,” Trump said. “They lost 65,000 in Vietnam.” Ashley Murray contributed to this report.

articles.title: DeepMind reveals Gemini Robotics 2.5 and open safety benchmark "ASIMOV-jailbreak"
articles.description: The new model is up to twice as successful at some tasks.
articles.content: Google DeepMind has revealed a new generation of the AI-powered Gemini Robotics platform. In the 2.5 release, Google says its robotic AI is getting tantalizingly close to completing real-world tasks as well as humans do. In fact, some Gemini robots were able to get actual work done in Mercedes-Benz factories, and the team is preparing for a day when robots operate alongside humans with an open source safety benchmark. DeepMind's physical AI platform has several computational layers between user input and robotic action. There's the vision-language model piece, which is Gemini Embodied Reasoning. Essentially, it takes your instructions and uses live video to plan how the robot can accomplish the task. The other main component is the vision-language-action (VLA) that actually generates robot actions, like moving an actuator—that's Gemini Robotics, which has been bumped to version 2.5. DeepMind says that Gemini Robotics 2.5 is much better at tasks that require a high degree of dexterity. The model was evaluated across more than 200 activities, including serving food with tongs and using a pipette, as you would see in a laboratory. Google also showed that Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid robot with Gemini Robotics 2.5 can now tie a bow with its five-fingered hands, a notable feat, because deformable objects (like ribbon) are notoriously difficult for robots to manipulate.Read full article Comments

See 70 swimmers brave the Great Lakes in honor of the Edmund Fitzgerald crew
articles.description: A new documentary chronicles a 38-day, 411-mile swim across the Great Lakes in honor of the 29 men who died on the Edmund Fitzgerald.
articles.content: Stage 1 swimmers (left to right), Joe Barr, Grant Combs, Daniel Chaffin, and Tammy Lenarz Carruth lay a wreath over the wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald.(Charlie Belk / Courtesy of Corey Adkins)In 2025, 70 swimmers attempted to complete the Edmund Fitzgerald’s journey across the Great Lakes. The legendary freighter sank during a storm on Lake Superior on Nov. 10, 1975.The feat is chronicled in a new documentary called, “We Finished Their Journey: The Story of the Edmund Fitzgerald Memorial Swim.” The film is available now in theatres and for streaming through the Great Lakes Shipwreck Historical Society.The Edmund Fitzgerald sank during a storm on Lake Superior on Nov. 10, 1975, killing all 29 men on board the ship. Last year, in honor of the 50th anniversary of the tragedy, a team of 70 swimmers attempted to complete the journey that those sailors started.The feat is chronicled in a new documentary called, “We Finished Their Journey: The Story of the Edmund Fitzgerald Memorial Swim.” The film will be available in theatres and for streaming through the Great Lakes Shipwreck Historical Society.Jim “The Shark” Dreyer, a record-setting open-water swimmer, served as the event director of the project. He started to develop the idea for the memorial swim in 2023 as he realized the 50th anniversary of the ship’s sinking was quickly approaching.“And I thought, 'We can't let this anniversary pass without doing something,'” he said. “Just something to help continue the legacy so that, you know, when it's 100 years, people are remembering the 29 men who perished.”The 411-mile journey began at the site of the shipwreck, and ended on Belle Isle in Detroit. 70 swimmers broke up the journey over 17 stages. The longest stretch spanned 35 miles across Lake Huron between the Upper and Lower Peninsula. Route of Edmund Fitzgerald Memorial Swim( Courtesy of Corey Adkins)“I've been organizing events for 30 years, but there's never been an event I've organized that that's had this many moving pieces,” Dreyer said.For 38 days, the swimmers were at the mercy of the Great Lakes. Some faced storms with waves as high as 15 feet. Others suffered sports injuries. Dreyer recalled one incident where a neighboring boat nearly collided with the swimmers.“You're always facing something that could be catastrophic when you're swimming on the Great Lakes,” Dreyer said.Corey Adkins, the producer and director of the documentary, remembered the mix of individuals who took part in the swim.“Everybody had a different personality. Every stage had a different personality,” Adkins said. “We had a guy named Smilin’ Mike. And Smilin’ Mike, I mean, you could probably hit him in the face and he'd still be smiling.”Another swimmer, Sheila Fitzgerald, was related to the ship’s namesake. She traveled from London to take part in the project.During the final stage of the swim, Adkins said, he continually texted updates to Heidi Wilhelm Brabon, whose father, Blaine Wilhelm, worked as an oiler on the Edmund Fitzgerald. Brabon was only 12 when the ship sank. She wanted to be one of the first to welcome the swimmers back to shore.An emotional greeting between Heidi Wilhelm Brabon, daughter of lost crewman Blaine Wilhelm, and Event Director Jim Dreyer at the Detroit finish.(Corey Adkins)“It just brought out, you know, everything good in humanity right there,” Adkins said. “People that actually cared about [Brabon’s] father and the other 28 people, guys that went down on the Fitzgerald.”Being able to greet Brabon at the finish line, Dreyer said, helped to cement the purpose of the project.“If anybody had any question as to the sincerity of the participants in this event, all they have to do is watch the finish, and see the emotion at the finish line, and see that it was real,” Dreyer said.How to watch 'We Finished Their Journey: The Story of the Edmund Fitzgerald Memorial Swim'When: Film premieres at 4 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026Where: Great Lakes Shipwreck Historical Society YouTube page and in select theatresFor more: Check the Great Lakes Shipwreck Museum website.

articles.title: FDA warns GLP-1 drugs may pose risk of rare condition that causes vision loss
articles.description: The risk appears small and data is mixed, but FDA wants patients to be aware.
articles.content: The Food and Drug Administration is warning that popular obesity drugs—including Ozempic, Wegovy, Zepbound, and Mounjaro—may carry a "potential increased risk" of a rare eye condition that can lead to permanent vision loss. In a drug safety communication Monday, the FDA said it will now require makers of GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs to add a warning about that risk on their drug labels. The specific eye condition it warns of is called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy or NAION. The condition is caused by restricted blood flow to the optic nerve, which leads to swelling and cell death and ultimately damages the nerve, causing abrupt vision loss that can often be permanent. It's unknown how GLP-1 drugs may cause NAION. The condition is rare overall, occurring in somewhere between two and 10 people in 100,000 in the general population, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology. These small numbers have made it more difficult to determine with certainty if there is a connection. Further complicating the potential link is the fact that the risk factors for developing NAION are common among patients taking GLP-1 drugs. The risk factors include diabetes, cardiovascular disease, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, metabolic syndrome, and obstructive sleep apnea.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Zohran Mamdani Visited MoMA’s West African Modern Architecture Survey and Loved It
articles.content: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has continued his social media campaign to stump for exhibitions staged by the city’s museums, this time focusing on a survey of West African modernist architecture at the Museum of Modern Art, whose praises he sang on Instagram early this morning. Titled “Architects of Liberation: Modernism in Western Africa,” the 400-work show surveys architectural projects in Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Togo, Benin, Nigeria, and Cameroon produced during a period of decolonization that began in some countries in the late 1950s. Curated by Martino Stierli and Ikem Stanley Okoye, the show features architectural models and archival imagery, as well as some contemporary artworks. Related Articles MoMA, Centre Pompidou, and M+ Will Treat Their Holdings as One Collection in Unprecedented Alliance MoMA to Stage Eva Hesse's First Major US Museum Exhibition in Two Decades “visited @themuseumofmodernart this weekend and am still thinking about their exhibition ‘architects of liberation: modernism in western africa,’” wrote Mamdani in his post. He specifically singled out Kader Attia’s 2014 sculpture Indépendence Tchao, a sculpture composed of rows of rusting index card boxes that the Algerian French artist obtained from a French colonial police headquarters. They are topped with a sign reading “HOTEL INDÉPENDENCE,” a reference to a similarly named hotel in Dakar, Senegal. Mamdani wrote that the sculpture asks the question: “to what extent were the visions of the independence era achieved?” It’s the second museum presentation Mamdani has posted about in the past month. In October, to celebrate his birthday, Mamdani visited the Studio Museum in Harlem, where he took in Taylor Simmons’s painting The Hypnotist (2026). Mamdani called the work by Simmons, a current participant in the museum’s storied artists-in-residence program, “just incredible.” The World's Premier Art Magazine since 1913. articles.title: Polestar has a new look with its Formula 2030 concept
articles.description: The shape looks like a Saab Aero-X, but the nose previews the next Polestar 2.
articles.content: Perhaps only a small percentage of Ars readers will care about the Polestar 2030 concept, debuted today by the electric automaker. Spun out of Volvo—once upon a time, Polestar was a racing team—the brand has leveraged the resources of parent-automaker Geely to create electric vehicles that marry a modern minimalist style with rewarding driving dynamics. But you now can’t buy any Polestars in the US, since Geely is Chinese, and banning Chinese-owned car brands enjoys remarkable bipartisan support in Congress. The Formula 2030 is about the same length as a Polestar 2 but with a very low roofline. If anything, the two-box shape reminds me of the Saab Aero-X, one of the final concepts from the then-terminal Swedish automaker. (In many ways, Polestar has adopted Saab’s mantle.) Credit: Polestar These rear lights will show up in production Polestars. In 2008, Saab showed off the Aero-X concept. Credit: Scott Barbour/Getty Images Polestar says the concept fits into its own segment somewhere between the next Polestar 2 and the Polestar 7—it numbers its cars chronologically (mostly), not based on size—although it’s not saying if the hatchback design will go into series production. Successfully packaging rear-seat passengers and a lithium-ion battery pack is something a concept needn’t worry about, after all. Rather, it’s a styling exercise, or more than one.Read full article Comments

Commentary: You have the floor. Now do the work.
articles.description: For Democrats taking on new responsibilities after this election, the message should be straightforward: You have the floor. Now it is up to you to act. Not every voter who supported you endorsed your entire platform. Some wanted a change in direction. Some wanted a check on power. Others simply wanted leaders to pay attention […]
articles.content: Michigan Democratic Party members and supporters watch election night returns on Nov. 3, 2026, at a watch party in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)For Democrats taking on new responsibilities after this election, the message should be straightforward: You have the floor. Now it is up to you to act. Not every voter who supported you endorsed your entire platform. Some wanted a change in direction. Some wanted a check on power. Others simply wanted leaders to pay attention to the pressures shaping their daily lives. The work ahead should center on priorities such as: Making everyday life more affordable, from groceries and utilities to housing and transportation. Improving access to affordable health care, including prescription drugs and mental health services. Strengthening economic opportunity so that work offers a realistic path to stability. Restoring trust in government through transparency, ethical conduct and meaningful accountability. Protecting democratic institutions and respecting the limits of public power. Addressing immigration with workable policies that take both public concerns and human dignity seriously. These are not problems that disappear when the campaign signs come down. Nor can they be solved by reminding voters how objectionable the other party is. Explain what you intend to do. Make the case for your proposals. Listen when people identify shortcomings. Work across party lines where progress is possible, and explain the disagreement honestly where it is not. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE No party can promise immediate solutions to every problem. But voters should be able to expect clear priorities, sustained effort and an honest accounting of what has and has not been accomplished. Republicans have responsibilities here, too. Losing an election does not excuse obstruction for its own sake, just as winning one does not excuse overreach. Both parties remain responsible for the people they represent. The lesson of all-or-nothing politics should not be that Democrats now get their turn to dismiss the opposition. It should be that the public deserves something better than another round of the same behavior. Michigan does not need its leaders to agree on everything. It needs them to take shared problems seriously enough to work through their differences. You asked for the opportunity to lead. Now give people something more valuable than another opponent to blame.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed launches Habibi PAC to build Democratic influence
articles.description: Just days after his election win, Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed launched a leadership PAC called Habibi Pac for what political commentators say is to fund political allies and build influence ahead of the 2028 elections.
articles.content: Abdul El-Sayed (middle) in a campaign photo in Detroit. (Campaign photo / Abdul for Senate)Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed launched a new leadership political action committee (PAC) named Habibi PAC. Habibi translates to "my friend" or "my beloved" in Arabic. PACs take in contributions and pool the money to support or oppose political campaigns. A leadership PAC is similar, but it's run by a politician specifically to raise money for other candidates, allowing them to fund their political allies. Political commentators view the immediate launch of Habibi PAC as a classic strategic move to help El-Sayed build influence within the Democratic Party and position himself as a key player ahead of the 2028 presidential election cycle.However, campaign finance watchdogs are keeping a close eye on the new committee. Neil Thanedar, executive director of the Michigan Campaign Finance Network (MCFN) , noted that because the PAC was launched less than a week ago, there is currently no Federal Election Commission (FEC) reporting available to show who is donating or how the money is being spent.Thanedar pointed out that El-Sayed's use of a PAC is notable given his stance against accepting certain PAC money during his Senate campaign. "It will be interesting to see who the donors are for this PAC and where the money goes, because Abdul El-Sayed has talked numerous times about not wanting to accept corporate PAC money and other special interest funding," Thanedar said.The Federal Election Commission (FEC) strictly prohibits candidates from using their official campaign committee funds for personal use. However, because a leadership PAC is legally considered a separate political committee, not the candidate's campaign committee, it has historically been used as a loophole regarding the "personal use" ban."So campaign accounts can strictly not be used for personal things," Thanedar said. "But the leadership PAC has this loophole where, in some cases, senators are paying for international trips, donating money to candidates in other countries... there is a lot of places where that money can go that is for the candidate's personal use, not for politics."He added that these committees can sometimes become a "honeypot for bad behavior," allowing donors to directly influence politicians who spend the PAC funds on luxury vacations or personal items. "I think a key factor of keeping politicians honest is seeing where is the money coming in from and where is the money going out."Because Habibi PAC is new, it is currently subject to a smaller donation limit that will increase once the PAC has been active for six months, received at least 51 donations, and contributed to five different candidates. Until those milestones are met, political observers and watchdogs will be waiting for the first FEC reports to see exactly who is funding the new senator's committee and where that money is going.

Ukraine’s fiber-optic drones get squeezed by AI data center demand
articles.description: Ukraine competes with Russia and data centers for China’s optical fiber supply.
articles.content: Impervious to battlefield jamming, drones physically connected to human operators by miles of fiber-optic cables have become such a common weapon of war in Ukraine that trees and fields are strewn with tangled cables thinner than fishing lines. But importing such fiber-optic material from China has become more costly as drone warfare’s needs compete with global demand from AI data centers for the same limited supply—and so Ukrainian drone makers have been adapting. Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, the Ukrainians have been forced out of necessity to continually develop battlefield innovations involving first-person view (FPV) quadcopter drones and other heavier types of drones. But it was the Russian military that first deployed unjammable fiber-optic drones to repel Ukrainian forces’ cross-border incursion into the Kursk Oblast in 2024. The Ukrainians quickly followed suit in developing their own fiber-optic drones, given the drones’ capability to shrug off electronic warfare jamming that could neutralize radio-controlled drones. Russia and Ukraine have relied on Chinese suppliers for some off-the-shelf drones and a wide array of drone components, including bulk orders of fiber wound around very large spools or sometimes small finished spools ready for installation on drones. The finished spools can hold enough fiber-optic cable for drones to regularly operate at ranges of dozens of miles, and sometimes up to 62 miles (100 kilometers) in extreme cases, as reported by the independent Russian publication The Insider.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Review: Apple's M6 MacBook Pro is good, but it's missing all the exciting stuff
articles.description: Per usual, the basic MacBook Pro lags behind the flagships where it counts.
articles.content: I've written more than once about the weird positioning of Apple's entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro, which has always occupied an uncomfortable perch between the MacBook Air and the higher-end MacBook Pros. The best versions of this laptop, like last year's M5 refresh, come with the same basic design and external features of the higher-end MacBook Pros, just with a more modest processor and a lower ceiling for specs like RAM and storage. The lesser versions stick with older designs or other compromises, reserving Apple's most updated designs and screen technologies for the more expensive high-end models. Recall the 13-inch M1 and M2 MacBook Pros, which stuck with Apple's 2016-era MacBook Pro designs for everything, up to and including the now-abandoned Touch Bar. (If you're someone at Apple maintaining Touch Bar support into the 2030s for the sake of these two laptop models, I'd like to hear from you. Not for a story! I'd just like to know how you are.) This year's entry-level MacBook Pro mostly falls into that latter category. It does get an Apple M6 chip, and the M6 is great—rumors suggest the M6 won't get Pro, Max, or Ultra configurations, so there are some fringe benefits here that you can't get in the top-tier MacBook Pros. But it uses the same MacBook Pro design Apple has been using since 2021. There's no touchscreen, no OLED panel, no Dynamic Island, no half-pound weight reduction, no glowing Apple logo on the lid.Read full article Comments

articles.title: WAV vs MP3: How to choose the right audio file format
articles.description: WAV vs MP3? Compare file size, sound quality, and compatibility, and learn which audio format to use for recording, editing, sharing, and voice cloning
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. Simply put, WAV (Waveform Audio File Format) is better for recording and editing because it is uncompressed and lossless, while MP3 (MPEG-1 Audio Layer III) is better for sharing and streaming as the files are much smaller. Choose WAV when audio quality matters most, and choose MP3 when file size and compatibility matter more. WAV is an uncompressed, lossless audio format. MP3 is a compressed, lossy audio format that removes audio detail to make the file smaller. WAV and MP3 are two of the most common file formats for audio projects, but they both have advantages and disadvantages. Before you hit export on your project, it helps to know where each audio file format shines. In this guide, we’ll compare WAV vs. MP3 files to help you choose the right format for your next audio project. Here’s an overview of the key differences between WAV and MP3 files. Uncompressed and lossless, preserves all original audio data Compressed and lossy, removes audio data to save space Highest possible audio quality and fidelity Very good, but small details may be missing Professional audio recording and editing, audio archives Both WAV and MP3 are file formats used for sharing audio recordings, but they work differently. The biggest difference between the two is lossless vs. lossy audio. A WAV file preserves the raw waveform from the original audio recording without removing any data. As it isn’t compressed, the audio’s details are still present with no losses. Due to that, WAV offers the best possible audio fidelity in a digital file. An MP3 file, on the other hand, compresses the audio recording to make the file smaller. It does this by using psychoacoustic compression to remove audio details that listeners are unlikely to hear or notice. While the overall audio quality is still very good, MP3 doesn’t provide the same audio fidelity and detail that WAV does. MP3 files can also range in quality depending on their bitrate. 320 kbps is the highest-quality bitrate for MP3s, providing very clear audio. Bitrates of 96 kbps or less are noticeably lower-quality. When creating an MP3 file, you can also choose between constant and variable bitrate. Constant bitrate files keep the audio quality the same across the entire recording. Variable bitrate files adjust the bitrate throughout the recording based on the complexity of the data, which delivers better audio quality for a given file size. In short, WAV keeps all the audio data, while MP3 trades some detail for a much smaller file. When selecting an audio file type for your projects, there are a few key factors to consider: file size, sound quality and fidelity, and compatibility with your workflows and audience. WAV files are much larger than MP3 files. One minute of CD-quality stereo audio (44.1 kHz, 16-bit) takes up about 10.6 MB as a WAV file, compared with about 0.96 MB as a 128 kbps MP3 and about 2.4 MB as a 320 kbps MP3. That makes a WAV file roughly 11 times larger than a 128 kbps MP3 and about 4.4 times larger than a 320 kbps MP3. If you’re creating audio content at scale, you could quickly run out of storage space using WAV files. WAV files are also more difficult to share because of their large size. They take much longer to upload and download than MP3s. Some email and messaging platforms also limit the sizes of attachment files, making them difficult to share through these platforms. WAV files have higher audio quality than MP3 files. As stated above, this is because they preserve the entire audio recording without removing any data, while MP3 files are compressed. That said, MP3 files still offer good audio quality, especially if they have a higher bitrate. For most casual listeners, the difference between an MP3 file and a WAV file is minimal. Another key factor to consider is file compatibility with your devices and the devices your audience is using. This is especially important if you’re exporting a project for a specific use case, like producing podcast audio to upload to a supported platform. MP3 files are compatible with virtually any device or software that streams audio, including smartphone apps, desktop web browsers, and stereo systems. WAV files are compatible with most modern devices and software platforms. However, some platforms may struggle to process a WAV’s large size efficiently. Some older stereo systems and streaming platforms do not support WAV files at all. If you plan on distributing a podcast or music file to a wide audience, an MP3 file is a more accessible option. WAV files are best for scenarios where audio quality and fidelity are your top priorities, and you have enough digital storage available for large audio files. When you’re recording and editing an audio project, it’s best to use WAV files to preserve audio quality. With a WAV file, you’ll be able to hear all the details in the audio as you’re editing to help you make informed creative decisions. If you edit with MP3 files, the audio will be compressed every time you save a new version or make a copy. Over time, this compression adds up, which affects the quality of the final product. Using WAV files through the editing process prevents this problem. WAV is also the best choice for projects like film and TV voiceovers, multi-track music production, or audio archives, where quality is essential. Choose WAV whenever you still plan to edit or archive the audio. MP3 files are best for sharing music, podcasts, and other audio files intended for a large audience. They’re compatible with a wide range of systems and streaming platforms for a convenient listening experience. You can also send MP3 files via email, whereas WAV files often exceed size limits. MP3 files are also best in situations where file storage space is limited. For example, if your team records hundreds of hours of podcast audio each month, it makes sense to store each file as an MP3 once you’re done editing to save space. Additionally, MP3 is the recommended file format for voice cloning samples. ElevenLabs recommends MP3 at 192 kbps or higher, and notes that WAV files usually don’t improve clone quality and can cause problems with the upload process. Use a clean recording with minimal background noise for the best results. If you’re uploading or sharing at scale, then MP3 is the way to go. Casual listeners usually won’t notice the difference in quality between a WAV file and an MP3 file, especially if the MP3 file has a high bitrate. That’s because MP3 compression removes details that are usually indistinguishable to the human ear. Higher audio quality and fidelity are most important during the recording and editing process but don't usually affect the streaming experience. To convert an MP3 file to a WAV file, use a digital file conversion tool. Adobe Express and Audacity are both popular tools that have built-in file conversion from MP3 to WAV. The conversion process will make the file significantly larger, so make sure you have enough storage space first. However, it’s important to note that converting an MP3 file to a WAV file won’t improve the audio quality. That’s because the conversion process can’t add back the data that was lost when the file was originally compressed. Some audio and video editing programs only accept WAV files and can’t import compressed formats such as MP3. In that case, convert the file before you edit, even though conversion won’t improve the audio quality. If you need a transcript of an MP3 or WAV file, you can use ElevenLabs’ MP3 to text and audio to text tools. WAV and MP3 are not your only options. FLAC and M4A are two other alternatives, both of which are offered as download options on ElevenLabs. FLAC is a lossless format. It compresses audio without discarding any data, which means a FLAC file sounds identical to the WAV it came from while typically taking up around half the space. The tradeoff is compatibility, as some editing tools and older devices support FLAC less widely than WAV or MP3. M4A is an audio file container that usually holds AAC-compressed audio. Like MP3, it is lossy, but AAC generally delivers similar or better quality than MP3 at the same bitrate, which makes M4A a good fit for Apple devices and podcasts. Some older players and software handle it less reliably than MP3. In ElevenLabs Text to Speech, the advanced download options include MP3 at 192 kbps and 256 kbps, M4A, and FLAC, alongside the standard 128 kbps MP3 and WAV. Choose FLAC when you want lossless quality at a smaller size than WAV, and choose M4A when you want a compact file for sharing. ElevenCreative helps you turn your ideas into real-life audio projects, including podcasts, audiobooks, and voiceovers. Use ElevenLabs’ AI models to turn text to speech or even clone your own voice for a more personalized experience. With ElevenCreative, you can also create custom music and sound effects for your audio projects. ElevenCreative Studio supports both MP3 and WAV exports. On the Free, Starter, and Creator plans, you can export a 128 kbps MP3 or a WAV generated from a 128 kbps source. On the Pro, Scale, Business, and Enterprise plans, you can export a 16-bit, 44.1 kHz WAV or a 192 kbps MP3 (Ultra Lossless). The export quality setting does not affect credit usage. You can also generate speech with Text to Speech and choose your download format there. Explore ElevenCreative to see Studio in action, or sign up today to start creating. You can convert an MP3 file to a WAV file using a digital file converter. However, the conversion process won’t restore the audio quality that was lost during the original MP3 compression process. DJs can use either file type, depending on their specific setup and goals. Many DJs use MP3 files because they take up less space, allowing them to carry a larger music library with them. However, some DJs prefer using WAV files on high-end speaker systems due to their fidelity. Most modern music players support both MP3 and WAV formats. However, exact compatibility depends on the specific device and software you’re using. WAV is better quality because it is uncompressed and keeps all the original audio data. A high-bitrate MP3 sounds very close to WAV for most listeners, so the difference matters most during recording and editing. WAV files are large, slow to upload and share, and often exceed email attachment limits. They also take up much more storage than MP3 files, and some older devices and platforms don’t support them. Spotify doesn’t stream in WAV or MP3. It uses other compressed formats and also offers lossless streaming on some plans, so check Spotify’s support pages for current details. articles.title: Introducing Scribe v3 and v3 Live, our most accurate speech to text models
articles.description: Scribe v3 and Scribe v3 Live are our most accurate speech to text models for recorded and realtime audio, with 27% fewer word errors than Scribe v2.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. Products built on audio start with a transcript: meeting notes, voice agents, dubbing, clinical documentation, and broadcast archives that span decades of content. Getting that transcript right the first time matters, because every error travels downstream, where it costs far more to fix. But real world audio is messy. It’s several people talking over each other in a meeting, a customer on a busy street who pauses halfway through a sentence, or a support call where neither person is speaking their first language. Today ElevenLabs is launching two new Speech to Text models built for exactly these conditions: Scribe v3 Live is available today in ElevenAgents. Both models are also available in ElevenAPI, where switching from Scribe v2 is a one-line change to the model ID. Scribe has powered hundreds of millions of hours of transcription for meeting-notes apps, contact centers, clinical documentation tools, and voice agents. Across use cases, the teams building on it kept asking for the same five things. Meeting and note-taking teams wanted better diarization in quick back-and-forth and with three or more speakers. Voice agent teams said a silence timer cuts callers off when they pause mid-sentence or slow down to read out a number. Teams building live products were giving up accuracy for speed, since realtime ran noticeably worse than batch. Customers in India wanted Hindi to match English, even when callers switch between the two mid-sentence. And many wanted more control over the output, from numbers written as “123” to key term lists long enough for a product catalog or a list of drug names. In a meeting transcript, identifying the right speaker matters just as much as getting the right words. Scribe v3 makes 17% fewer diarization errors than Scribe v2 on recordings with three or more speakers, which are the recordings where most existing models fail. Scribe v3 Live also brings diarization to realtime transcription for the first time, with 39% fewer diarization errors than the next-best realtime model we tested. For conversations to feel natural, voice agents need to accurately predict when a speaker is done talking. Traditional turn-taking systems do so based on periods of silence. But silence alone forces a trade-off: setting a short threshold could interrupt people who pause in the middle of a sentence and a long one makes an agent feel slow. Scribe v3 Live uses the context of the conversation as well as the audio, so a caller who pauses halfway through a number isn’t cut off. This is the same turn detection ElevenAgents already uses, now available in ElevenAPI. Scribe v3 can infer hints about which languages a recording may contain and lets you choose whether numbers return as digits or words. Keyterm prompting takes up to 1,000 terms you know will come up, such as brand names, acronyms and jargon, and transcript edits apply formatting rules written in plain English, such as “write every date as YYYY-MM-DD.” Scribe v3 Live adds a multilingual mode for conversations that switch languages mid-sentence. It also adds a keyterm library for vocabularies too large for a list. Where keyterm prompting covers terms you know will come up, keyterm library holds thousands that might, and the model consults it only when it hears a likely match. ElevenLabs evaluated both models against Scribe v2, Scribe v2 Realtime, and other popular Speech to Text models, scoring each on the same datasets. Multilingual accuracy was measured on an internal version of the FLEURS benchmark, which tests short, clean read speech in 102 languages. FLEURS can’t measure diarization, since every clip has one speaker, so we also built our own dataset of real meetings, agent calls, and voice notes across 16 languages. We’ll be open sourcing this soon. Scribe v3 has the lowest diarization error of any model we tested, with 12% fewer errors than Scribe v2 overall and 17% fewer on recordings with three or more speakers. We report word error rate (WER) alongside semantic WER, which counts an error only when the meaning of the transcript changes. Across 102 languages on FLEURS, Scribe v3 reduces WER by 27% compared with Scribe v2 and improves in every language tested. In languages easier to transcribe, German improved by 42%, Spanish by 35%, and English by 23%. The improvements are larger in languages that are harder to transcribe: Swahili drops by 34%, Tamil by 29%, and Thai by 28%. Scribe v3 also makes fewer word errors than every other batch (non-streaming) model we tested, comparing each one on the languages both models support. On the English portion of our 16-language real-world dataset, Scribe v3 Live has a diarization error rate of 3.1%, compared with 5.9% to 7.3% for the other realtime models we tested. Standard diarization scores also count transcription mistakes, such as missed words, and realtime models miss more words than batch models. To measure only whether each word was given to the right speaker, we aligned each model’s transcript to the reference before scoring. This lowers every model’s error rate, so these results can’t be compared with the batch diarization results above. For realtime models we lead with semantic WER. A streaming model writes text before it has heard the whole sentence, and each provider formats numbers, punctuation and casing differently as it goes. Standard WER counts those differences as errors even when the meaning is the same, so semantic WER is the fairer comparison. Across 102 languages, Scribe v3 Live reduces semantic WER by 43% and WER by 31% compared with Scribe v2 Realtime. It improves in every language, and has a lower error rate than every other realtime model we tested. The improvements are largest where realtime transcription has lagged: Greek improves by 77%, Danish by 54%, and Croatian by 45%, while Hindi improves by 36%. A note on method: we scored each language on its own before averaging, so all 102 languages count equally. Many published results pool every clip into a single score, which tends to give lower numbers, so results measured in different ways aren’t directly comparable. Every model launch comes with percentages, this one included, and on paper, it’s difficult to discern what a few points mean in real-world scenarios. A one-hour meeting at 150 words per minute is about 9,000 words, so the gap between a 4% and a 2% word error rate is 180 wrong words, three for every minute someone was talking. Diarization error is measured in time rather than words so in that same meeting, every point is 36 seconds of speech under the wrong name. What those errors cost depends on where they land. In a podcast transcript a wrong word is a typo, but on an earnings call “fifteen” heard as “fifty” ends up in an analyst’s model. Errors also cluster in names, numbers, acronyms and jargon, which are exactly the words a summary or an agent most needs to get right. Voice agents feel this most, because a single misheard digit can fail the check that starts the call. Eneco, which supplies energy to more than 2 million homes and businesses in the Netherlands, runs its voice agent on ElevenAgents and tested Scribe v3 Live on it ahead of launch. In real customer calls, the agent recognized Dutch postcodes correctly on the first try 40% more often, and house numbers 15% more often. “ElevenLabs is a true partner for Eneco. Together with their forward deployed engineers, we are working to further improve our voice agent,” said Ruud Huigsloot, a Senior Product Manager at Eneco. “It’s great to see significant results this early, and we are excited to continue collaborating.” Scribe v3 and Scribe v3 Live run in the US by default, and are offered in isolated EU, India, and Singapore environments for enterprise customers with data residency requirements. Zero Retention Mode deletes audio and text as soon as a request completes. Both models are covered by our SOC 2, ISO 27001, and PCI DSS Level 1 programs, are HIPAA-eligible with a Business Associate Agreement, and are available for private deployment. Scribe v3 Live is available in ElevenAgents, and both v3 and v3 Live are the default in the ElevenLabs app. Sign up to try it. Both models are also available in ElevenAPI today. Existing integrations upgrade by changing the model ID to scribe_v3 or scribe_v3_live. For healthcare teams, we’re also releasing a version of Scribe v3 Live optimized for medical conversations in ElevenAgents. Create with the highest quality AI Audio
