articles.title: Syrian Arab Republic launches coordinated public health response following poliovirus detection in Deir Ezzor
articles.content: 9 November 2026, Damascus, Syrian Arab Republic – The Ministry of Health is strengthening vaccination and surveillance activities to protect children following the detection of poliovirus type 1 (VDPV1) in two children aged between 6 and 13 months who developed paralysis in Deir Ezzor Governorate. The Ministry, supported by the World Health Organization (WHO), the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and other partners, has already begun vaccination activities in affected areas and is preparing further campaigns. Families are encouraged to check their children’s vaccination records, complete all recommended doses and participate in campaigns targeting their children. Polio can cause permanent paralysis, but it can be prevented through vaccination. Completing the recommended doses helps protect children, and high vaccination coverage helps stop the virus from spreading. Additional doses offered during campaigns strengthen protection; they do not replace routine childhood vaccinations. Disruptions to health services and difficulties accessing routine immunization have left gaps in protection in some communities. The response focuses on reaching children who have missed vaccinations and on helping families access reliable information and essential health services. Following initial reports of suspected cases on 11 October 2026, health teams conducted a vaccination campaign on 18 October, reaching more than 34 000 children under five in affected areas of Deir Ezzor. A further campaign is planned for next week, with additional rounds and locations to be determined through ongoing assessments. The Ministry will announce the areas covered, eligible age groups and how families can access vaccination services. “Vaccination is one of the most important steps families can take to protect their children from polio. We encourage parents and caregivers to complete their children’s recommended vaccinations and cooperate with health teams during upcoming campaigns,” said Syrian Minister of Health Dr Mousab Al Ali. “Our responsibility is to reach children who need protection and keep the public informed. We will provide regular updates on the situation and our response. The awareness and cooperation of our communities is essential to these efforts.” The Ministry, with support from WHO, UNICEF and partners, is strengthening surveillance and conducting field investigations to identify any further cases, assess the risk of transmission and guide vaccination activities. Alongside this response, efforts continue to restore essential health services. The number of operational primary health care centres in Deir Ezzor has increased from 40 to 87, and the plan is to increase the number to 124 to help more families access routine immunization and primary care. Particular attention is being given to communities that have faced prolonged difficulties accessing services so that children can receive care regardless of where they live. Syria’s experience in stopping poliovirus outbreaks in the past, including during years of conflict, underscores the value of coordinated health action and community participation in protecting children. “Polio can be stopped, but we must close immunity gaps and reach every child. WHO is working with the Ministry of Health and partners to support a rapid, coordinated response,” said WHO Representative in Syria Dr Caroline Clarinval. “Every child deserves protection from preventable diseases, including polio. UNICEF remains committed to supporting the Ministry of Health and partners in strengthening immunization services and ensuring that no child is left behind,” said UNICEF Representative in Syria Meritxell Relaño Arana. The Ministry will provide regular public updates on the epidemiological situation, response activities and upcoming vaccination campaigns. Updates will distinguish confirmed findings from information still under investigation and explain any changes to the response as assessments progress. The Ministry of Health, WHO, UNICEF and partners will continue working together to stop poliovirus transmission, strengthen routine immunization and support sustained access to essential health services across Syria. articles.description: Sweeping Democratic election wins could advance abortion access in states with tight restrictions, especially in Georgia, Iowa and Texas, where Democrats seized the governor’s office for the first time in decades. articles.content: Georgia Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms spoke last week at the state Capitol about her transition into office. In Georgia, Iowa and Texas, sweeping Democratic election wins could advance abortion access. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)Sweeping Democratic election wins could advance abortion access in states with tight restrictions, especially in Georgia, Iowa and Texas, where Democrats seized the governor’s office for the first time in decades. All three states will have Democratic attorneys general, and in Georgia and Texas, Democrats will control the state House while Republicans retain the state Senate. Texas has a strict abortion ban, while Iowa and Georgia only allow it up to about six weeks of pregnancy. Meanwhile, in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, Democrats have won new “trifectas” — control of the governor’s office and both legislative chambers — creating new opportunities to expand abortion rights. Both Pennsylvania Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and Wisconsin Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley have already pledged to codify abortion rights through state law or constitutional amendment. Abortion rights supporters also won victories in three of the four states — Missouri, Nevada and Virginia — where abortion-related measures were on the ballot. The lone exception was Idaho, where voters preserved their state’s strict abortion ban. State consequences are already on display in Texas, where Democratic Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson has promised to stop suing telehealth abortion providers in other states. Johnson’s proclamation is a stark reversal of the policy of his Republican predecessor, Ken Paxton, who failed in his bid to become a U.S. senator. “My hope in humanity has been restored a little bit, and I don’t think I even realized how much that was wearing on me behind the scenes for the last two years,” said Kaitlyn Kash, who left Texas in 2021 to obtain an abortion in Kansas after fatal fetal complications threatened her pregnancy and potentially her own health. Kash was among several plaintiffs who joined the 2023 Zurawski v. Texas lawsuit seeking to clarify the state’s medical emergency exceptions to its abortion ban. In 2024, the Texas Supreme Court ruled 9-0 in favor of the state. But future abortion cases could see different outcomes: Last week, Democrats won all four Texas Supreme Court seats that were up for election. That leaves the GOP with a narrow 5-4 advantage on the state Supreme Court. “To not have a vindictive attorney general anymore is going to save lives,” Kash said, referring to actions Paxton has taken, including bringing legal actions against abortion providers inside and outside the state and petitioning the state Supreme Court to halt a court ruling allowing the termination of a nonviable pregnancy. Less impact in Washington Despite huge Democratic gains in Congress, the change at the federal level is likely to be less significant, at least in the short term. President Donald Trump won’t leave office until January 2029, and Democrats did not win a filibuster-proof 60 seats in the Senate, let alone the two-thirds majority in the House and Senate they would need to override a presidential veto. “As long as Trump holds executive and veto powers, we have more work than celebrating to do,” said Brittany Fonteno, president and CEO of the National Abortion Federation in a written statement. “The next two years will be a critical time to prepare for the kind of governing power that will deliver real and lasting reproductive freedom.” Nevertheless, national abortion rights leaders have signaled high expectations for candidates they helped send to Congress, and they want Democrats to fight to preserve telehealth abortion. If Dr. Heidi Overton, Trump’s controversial pick to oversee the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, is not confirmed during the upcoming lame duck session, abortion-rights advocates will look to the new Democratic-dominated Senate to block her nomination. “The Senate just became the backstop,” said Gowri Buddiga, campaign director of Free & Just, an abortion rights advocacy group, in a written statement. “An FDA nominee who’s spent years calling medication abortion dangerous now has to get past a chamber that’s heard from the women these bans have hurt.” Unlike the 2022 midterms, which were held just months after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the federal right to an abortion, there is debate over just how important abortion was in this election. According to an exit poll conducted for The Associated Press, 39% of voters cited the economy as their top issue, 33% said it was the state of American democracy and 14% pointed to immigration. No other issue broke single digits and abortion was not among the top six. But abortion law expert Mary Ziegler said that while abortion appears to have been less of a top-of-mind issue this year, that’s not because voters care less about it. “It’s that there was nothing happening with abortion right now, and that isn’t just a fun coincidence,” said Ziegler, a professor at UC Davis School of Law. “That’s because the Trump administration has been trying really hard to kick down the road any litigation or federal restrictions that would have made it front of mind for voters again.” Ziegler said there are certain avenues that congressional Democrats could explore to expand access to abortion federally. Even if those efforts fail, she said, they might benefit Democrats politically leading up to the next presidential election in 2028. “While Republicans have successfully drawn attention away from abortion, they haven’t really actually made abortion a good issue for Republicans,” she said. “So I don’t see what the harm would be in passing a bill that would be popular and having Trump veto it and have J.D. Vance and Marco Rubio have to defend it, because it’s been very good for Republicans not to have to talk about this issue at all.” For their part, anti-abortion organizations have blamed Republicans and Trump for not campaigning on the issue and ignoring an important voting base, pointing to the highly funded and victorious anti-abortion win in Idaho as evidence. “Let’s be clear: the GOP didn’t run on abortion in 2026. It ran an ostrich campaign: a big elephant with its head buried in the sand,” wrote Students for Life of America President Kristan Hawkins in a subscriber email the day after Election Day. Hawkins also noted that several prominent Republican congressional candidates who said they supported abortion rights, including U.S. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, U.S. Rep. Mike Lawler of New York and U.S. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, lost their seats. Storytelling strategy Abortion rights advocates argue that many voters were moved by the personal stories they heard from candidates and their surrogates. On the campaign trail in Texas, Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa talked about her own nonviable pregnancy and argued that women and families should be able to make their own reproductive health decisions. She has publicly supported ending Texas’ abortion ban and restoring abortion access, a steep challenge given that Republicans still control the state Senate. In Georgia, Turiya Tomlin-Randall campaigned for Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms and Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff, who was reelected. Tomlin-Randall lives in Kansas City, Missouri, but her sister Candi Miller was living in Georgia in 2022 when she became pregnant. Miller and her husband had three kids and Miller had lupus, diabetes and hypertension, which made pregnancy dangerous. But she was terrified of getting into legal trouble after Georgia passed its new law. She ordered abortion pills online, but when she started experiencing a life-threatening infection, she was too scared to go to the hospital and died at home in November 2022. Tomlin-Randall said she only learned two years later that her sister’s death was connected to the state’s abortion law, because of ProPublica’s reporting on deaths related to abortion bans in Georgia and Texas. “This journey has taught me so much more about the effects of the ban,” said Tomlin-Randall, who is now raising two of the three children Miller left behind. “I’ve learned that most women who have abortions aren’t having abortions because they just don’t want to have a child. A lot of the women that I’ve encountered had to have abortions for their own safety.” Tomlin-Randall said she’s hopeful Bottoms will be a vocal advocate for abortion rights. Georgia Democratic Attorney General-elect Tanya Miller also has opposed the state’s six-week abortion ban and promised to defend access to legal reproductive health care. Miller defeated a prominent anti-abortion lawmaker in her race. Lauren Peterson, co-founder and CEO of Abortion in America, which organizes storytellers and advocates for abortion rights, called abortion the “unsung hero” of this election. She said abortion storytelling is an effective political strategy. “Our work is not over,” Peterson said. “Even in states where we won, we are going to have to now do the important work of holding people accountable to the promises they made.” Stateline reporter Sofia Resnick can be reached at sresnick@stateline.org. Introducing Businesses in ChatGPT
articles.description: Manage your business information, get insights about how your business shows up, and turn interest into action in ChatGPT.
articles.content: Claim your business, keep your information current, and understand how people engage with you in ChatGPT We’re introducing Businesses in ChatGPT in beta, giving businesses a new way to connect with the 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT each week. Through Business Hub(opens in a new window), businesses can claim their business, manage their information, and see insights on how people engage with them on ChatGPT. In addition, we are adding a powerful new way for businesses to interact with users via Business Agents, starting with eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the U.S. Together, these products create more ways for businesses to connect with people as they explore options and make decisions. They strengthen how people discover and interact with businesses in ChatGPT through broader business coverage, up-to-date information, and the ability to connect with a business through its Business Agent. Throughout these experiences, protecting the trust people place in ChatGPT remains our North Star. In Business Hub, companies can claim their organization in ChatGPT and, once verified, update key details and add self-service product feeds with pricing and availability. This gives businesses a new way to provide information to ChatGPT, helping people explore products and services using the most accurate and up-to-date details. Any eligible business located where ChatGPT is available can claim their business in ChatGPT through Business Hub. Existing OpenAI Enterprise customers and advertisers can work directly with their OpenAI representative to claim their business. Shopify merchants can connect their store from Business Hub or the Shopify admin to streamline verification. Eligible products from Shopify merchants are already integrated into ChatGPT through Shopify Catalog. Business Hub provides aggregated insights into how people engage with a business in ChatGPT. This includes the number of mentions and website clicks a business receives. Businesses can also explore discovery topics—common themes across conversations where their website is cited. These insights can help businesses understand how they’re represented and find opportunities to improve the information they share. We’ve designed these insights to protect user privacy. We don’t share users’ conversations or Business Agent chats with businesses. Insights are aggregated and are only available when there are enough conversations or interactions to meet certain thresholds. After claiming their business in ChatGPT, eligible organizations can build, test, and launch a Business Agent—a new way to answer questions and help people explore their offerings. When a business appears in a model response, people can click to see the business’s ChatGPT profile. If a Business Agent is available, customers can choose to start a conversation with the business to explore its offerings and ask follow-up questions. For example, someone comparing products could ask about the differences between two options and which features fit their needs. A Business Agent could help them explore those questions using the business’s information. For customers, this can make it easier to understand whether an offering is the right fit. For businesses, it creates a way to help interested customers learn more through a personalized conversation. The Business Agent conversation is clearly labeled, separate from the customer’s original ChatGPT conversation, and distinct from ChatGPT’s independent answers. Businesses can also sponsor their Business Agent and use it as the destination for ChatGPT Ads to reach more potential customers. Sponsored placements are clearly labeled and separate from ChatGPT responses. Business Agents are now available to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the United States. Learn more about eligible categories here. As people turn to AI to discover products, compare options and make decisions, ChatGPT has become the platform for people and businesses to connect through AI. Today’s announcement is an early step in bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT. We’re starting with the foundations: accurate business information, useful insights, and conversations that help people make informed decisions. Over time, we plan to expand Businesses in ChatGPT and Business Agents to more markets and business categories, and build tools for organizations with more complex needs. As the platform evolves, we’ll explore more ways for businesses to connect with customers—directly or through agents—in ChatGPT and beyond. Our goal is to make ChatGPT more useful for people making decisions, and give businesses new ways to participate and grow. Learn more and claim your business in ChatGPT.

Closing the AI guidance gap in education
articles.description: New ThinkYoung research and lessons from OpenAI’s EMEA education partnerships on supporting teachers, AI literacy, and independent learning.
articles.content: Drawing on new ThinkYoung research and lessons from our EMEA partnerships to support independent learning with AI. AI is prompting a fundamental reassessment of what education should prepare societies for. As intelligence becomes easier to access and apply, the question is no longer simply what people need to know, but which skills and capabilities will help them thrive in an AI-enabled world. Recent debates around PISA and AI, including those led by the OECD’s Andreas Schleicher(opens in a new window), underscore this shift. They also point to a central lesson: as AI becomes more capable, the role of teachers becomes more important, not less. Their expertise, judgement and ability to guide learning remain essential. Equipping teachers, schools and governments with AI skills and confidence to make informed decisions about these tools must therefore be a priority for education systems. Across EMEA, we are working with governments and education systems, including in Estonia, Slovakia, Greece and Italy, amongst others to explore how AI can support educators. These collaborations share three priorities: equitable access to frontier AI tools, jointly designed AI literacy programmes, and ongoing measurement and evaluation, whilst adapting to local languages, curricula and institutions. This report shares emerging lessons from our education partnerships in EMEA, focusing on educator support, AI literacy, local capability and evaluation. It examines what partners have tried, what they have reported and what remains uncertain. Country examples reflect their particular contexts and arrangements, and their findings should be interpreted within those limits. Five themes organise these lessons: clear educational goals, educator preparation, local partnerships, critical AI literacy and credible evidence. Three early patterns are emerging from this work: Country partnerships offer context-specific lessons. Experiences in Estonia, Greece and Slovakia point to three lessons that other education systems can apply: strong public leadership to set a clear direction, investment in teachers' skills and confidence, and practical support tailored to local curricula and classroom needs. While implementation will vary across countries, these principles offer a useful foundation for governments seeking to integrate AI responsibly and at scale. Closing the AI guidance gap in education is becoming increasingly urgent. New research from ThinkYoung,(opens in a new window) which examines the ways teachers and students are already engaging with AI highlights a clear guidance gap: 79% of surveyed students reported using AI for homework or assignments, but only 47% reported being shown how. Governments need to support educators and give students clearer expectations. Below we set out how educators can be better supported to set the terms and conditions of use. Early benefits for teachers are clear. Adoption and reported time savings for teachers are encouraging. Understanding where AI strengthens knowledge, independent thinking and retention requires sustained evaluation and through the government actions that we observed, we identify how to prioritise more research into this critical area. Our aim is to share practical lessons from these partnerships that education leaders can consider in their own contexts. These are early experiences, rather than a single model for education systems to follow. We are also learning how to judge progress with evidence: teacher adoption and reported time savings offer encouraging early signals. Surveys, programme monitoring and consultation help us understand participants’ experiences and the barriers they encounter. At OpenAI, our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits everyone. Helping learners flourish is central to that ambition. We believe that every young person should have the opportunity to develop the skills to participate in a world increasingly shaped by AI, whatever their background or wherever they attend school. We have a responsibility to contribute to that evidence and learn openly from the findings, including when they challenge our assumptions. Through the OpenAI Learning Lab, we are bringing education researchers together to understand when and how AI can support education systems. The choices made today will shape how the next generation learns, works and participates in society. With ambition, care, public leadership and a commitment to evidence, AI can help extend educational opportunity and strengthen young people’s capacity to understand, create and act for themselves.

articles.title: WHO launches “Together for Science and Health” movement to strengthen trust worldwide
articles.content: The World Health Organization (WHO) today launched Together for Science and Health, a new global movement uniting more than 240 organizations behind a shared commitment to strengthen trust in science and harness its power to improve health and development. With an official launch on World Science Day for Peace and Development, the movement rallies scientists, leaders, policy-makers and institutions across sectors, with 12 events taking place across countries and regions to mark the occasion. The launch is also closely associated with the Paris Peace Forum (PPF), one of France's flagship platforms for international diplomacy and multilateral cooperation, reflecting the country's commitment to mobilizing global actors around shared challenges. WHO Director-General, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, and French President Emmanuel Macron are leading the launch. “Science is one of humanity’s most powerful tools, and has always been the engine of better health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “Science has enabled people to live longer, healthier lives through vaccines, medicines, disease prevention and outbreak response. Through the Together for Science and Health Movement, WHO and partners are working together to champion evidence, trust and innovation as the foundations of healthier societies.” The movement will drive collective action around three priorities: bringing science and society closer together; strengthening the use of evidence in health policy-making; and improving how science is communicated and discussed. Participating organizations will share effective approaches, resources and lessons and build practical collaborations that strengthen trust and help ensure that scientific progress benefits everyone. Science shapes our health every day, from detecting and preventing diseases to developing new medicines, responding to outbreaks, and improving care. Many of the greatest advances in health have been possible because people, families, and communities have had confidence in scientific evidence and supported its translation into action. “No institution, country or community can build and sustain trust alone. The Together for Science and Health movement offers a space for dialogue and collaboration, not polarization. Shaping the future of science is the responsibility of everyone,” said Dr Sylvie Briand, WHO Chief Scientist and Assistant Director-General a.i. for Health Systems, Access and Data. “The movement will bring a wide range of stakeholders together around the idea that science is a shared resource that can help us build healthier, fairer and more resilient societies.” Rapid technological change and artificial intelligence are fast transforming how people access, interpret and share scientific and health information. Together for Science and Health will strengthen connections between science and society, helping people engage with evidence and use it with confidence. With today’s launch, WHO is inviting organizations and institutions worldwide to join the movement, contribute with their expertise and networks, and help build a future in which trusted science translates into better health for everyone. Dedicated to the well-being of all people and guided by science, WHO leads and champions global efforts to give everyone, everywhere, an equal chance at a safe and healthy life. We are the United Nations’ agency for health that connects nations, partners and people in more than 150 locations – leading the world’s response to health emergencies, preventing disease, addressing the root causes of health issues and expanding access to medicines and health care. Our mission is to support all countries to promote, provide and protect health. “Together for health. Stand with science”, the theme of World Health Day 2026, marks a year-long campaign to highlight science as the foundation for protecting health and well-being worldwide.
